title: A Reputation-Based Vesting Mechanism for Decentralized Autonomous Organizations
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Macau University of Science and Technology and Chinese Academy of Sciences - Institute of Automation

detail.title: A Reputation-Based Vesting Mechanism for Decentralized Autonomous Organizations
detail.abstract: In Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs), the lack of centralized authority makes it particularly difficult to incentivize high-quality contributions. Existing mechanisms mostly adopt one-time rewards, which are prone to inducing short-term speculative behaviors. To address this issue, a novel reputation-based vesting mechanism is proposed in the context of an infinitely repeated decentralized collaboration game. In this design, participants receive an immediate reward based on their current reputation, with the remainder vested for future release. The release conditions are strictly tied to their continued submission and production of valid outputs. The proposed mechanism is then demonstrated to provide incentive compatibility, Sybil resistance, and collusion resistance. Furthermore, computational experiments are conducted to validate the vesting mechanism, and results show that it can achieve endogenous security without relying on centralized identity verification or external enforcement.

title: The Impact of Agricultural Corporate Social Responsibility Transparency on Consumers' Impulse Buying
affiliations: South China Agricultural University, South China Agricultural University, South China Agricultural University and South China Normal University

detail.title: The Impact of Agricultural Corporate Social Responsibility Transparency on Consumers' Impulse Buying
detail.abstract: In the face of information asymmetry and trust deficits in agricultural markets, enhancing the transparency of agricultural corporate social responsibility (ACSR) has become a key strategy for alleviating consumer concerns. However, few studies have examined how this transparency influences consumers' impulse purchasing behaviour. Based on the S-O-R framework, this study integrates signalling theory, ABC theory and stakeholder theory to construct a multidimensional, dual-path model of transparency that drives impulse purchases. This model operates through two distinct pathways: the hedonic pathway, which involves immediate satisfaction, and the moral pathway, which involves indirect reciprocity. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was used to analyse the path effects of 772 consumer questionnaire responses, while necessity condition analysis (NCA) examined the necessity of transparency dimensions and psychological mediators. The results indicate that information accuracy, comprehensibility and timeliness play a critical role in both pathways, while objectivity primarily influences impulse purchases through immediate satisfaction. Consumers' prosocial behavioural traits significantly enhance the effect of psychological mechanisms on behavioural conversion. NCA results further confirm that specific transparency dimensions and psychological mediators are necessary conditions for impulse purchase. This study is the first to reveal the operational mechanism of ”transparency—psychological mechanisms—impulse purchasing” from both sufficiency and necessity perspectives, providing theoretical and empirical foundations for agricultural enterprises to optimize their CSR disclosure strategies.

title: Cultural value orientations and consumers' intentions to use augmented reality in online shopping: A cross-national study among young consumers
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Poznań University of Economics and Business, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Yonsei University and University of New Haven

detail.title: Cultural value orientations and consumers' intentions to use augmented reality in online shopping: A cross-national study among young consumers
detail.abstract: This study examines how individual-level cultural value orientations relate to consumers’ behavioral intentions (BI) to use augmented reality (AR) in online shopping. Although AR is increasingly used in e-commerce to support product visualization, product evaluation, and customer engagement, cross-national research provides limited direct evidence about how individual-level cultural orientations relate to its acceptance. To address this gap, data were collected through a CAWI survey following standardized AR try-on exposure among young consumers in Poland, the United States, and South Korea (N = 668). Cultural values were measured using individual-level scales based on Hofstede’s framework and analyzed with PLS-SEM.The results reveal an uneven pattern across samples. Individualism is the strongest positive correlate of BI in the U.S. sample, whereas uncertainty avoidance and long-term orientation are the most salient correlates in the Korean sample. Power distance and masculinity show little relevance across samples, while indulgence is positively associated with BI only in Korea. Overall, the findings suggest that cultural value orientations matter for AR use intention, but not all dimensions matter equally and their relevance depends on the shopping context and national setting. The study contributes to AR retail research by shifting attention from broad country-level cultural background to individual-level value orientations and by showing which dimensions appear more useful than others in explaining adoption in this setting.

title: A Study of the Effect of Types of Organizational Culture on Information Security Procedural Countermeasures

detail.title: A Study of the Effect of Types of Organizational Culture on Information Security Procedural Countermeasures

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study received IRB exemption from Nova Southeastern University (Protocol Number 2021-532, approved December 15, 2021, Exempt Category 2).

detail.abstract:
This study examined the impact of specific organizational cultures on information security procedural countermeasures (ISPC). With increasing security incidents and data breaches, organizations acknowledge that people are their greatest asset as well as a vulnerability. Previous research into information security procedural controls has centered on behavioral, cognitive, and social theories; some literature incorporates general notions of organization culture yet there is still an absence in socio-organizational studies dedicated to elucidating how information security policy (ISP) compliance can be augmented by implementing comprehensive security education, training, and awareness (SETA) programs focusing on education, training, and awareness initiatives.

A theoretical model was developed to examine the effect of types of organizational culture on ISPC. The types of organizational culture were bureaucratic, competitive, participative, and learning culture.

To evaluate the reliability of the model, a survey was conducted by Centiment utilizing responses from its panel. The types of organizational culture and ISPC were from well-known scales derived from the literature. Data were collected from the subjects using an online survey form with a Likert scale and demographic data such as age, gender, education, industry, and size of organization.

Data analysis showed bureaucratic organizational culture significantly influenced both ISP and SETA, but the effect was positive instead of negative as hypothesized. Learning organizational culture had a significant positive effect on SETA. Both competitive organizational culture and participative culture did not have a significant effect on ISP or SETA. Learning organizational culture did not have a significant effect on ISP. This study added to the body of knowledge by adding a socio-organization aspect to understanding employees’ non-compliance and adherence to ISP and SETA. The study revealed a correlation between socio-organizational understanding and compliance to ISP and SETA. As such, better policies and training can be produced with less detrimental influence for organizations looking to follow regulations efficiently.

title: Mapping and Comparing National Artificial Intelligence Strategies Across Africa: A Scoping Review
affiliations: Engineering Institute of Technology

detail.title: Mapping and Comparing National Artificial Intelligence Strategies Across Africa: A Scoping Review
detail.abstract:
Background: Africa is experiencing a rapid proliferation of national artificial intelligence (AI) strategies. Between 2018 and March 2026, seventeen African countries have published or formally adopted dedicated national AI strategies or policies. Despite this momentum, no comprehensive comparative scoping review has systematically mapped the content, architecture, ethical commitments, governance models, implementation readiness, or regional distribution of these strategies. Such a review is essential to guide continental harmonisation efforts and identify enduring policy gaps.

 Objective: To map, describe, and thematically compare national AI strategies adopted across African countries; assess their content depth using a novel instrument, the National AI Strategy Policy Depth Index (NAISPDI); classify implementation readiness using a four-level maturity scale; and identify continental policy gaps and future research priorities.

Methods: This review followed the five-stage scoping review framework of Arksey and O'Malley (2005), refined by Levac, Colquhoun, and O'Brien (2010), and was reported in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) checklist (Tricco et al., 2018). Sources included government strategy documents, grey literature, multilateral organisation reports, peer-reviewed articles, and reputable policy databases published between January 2021 and March 2026.

Results: Seventeen countries were included: Algeria, Benin, Cote d'Ivoire, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Mauritania, Mauritius, Morocco, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Senegal, Tunisia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Thematic analysis identified seven cross-cutting domains: governance models, strategic pillars, ethical frameworks, priority sectors, digital sovereignty, implementation readiness, and regional convergence and divergence. Application of the NAISPDI (scored 0-100) revealed wide variation in policy depth, ranging from 30 to 84. Only four countries (Egypt, Rwanda, Kenya, and Senegal) achieved high-maturity (Level 3-4) classification on the implementation readiness scale. North Africa demonstrates the most advanced governance architectures; East Africa shows greatest strategic ambition; West Africa the widest variation; and Southern Africa the strongest infrastructure base.

Conclusions: African AI strategies share a development-centric orientation and broadly converge around priority sectors of healthcare, agriculture, education, and public service delivery. However, significant gaps persist in binding ethical regulation, domestic financing, data governance, AI talent pipelines, and regional interoperability. The NAISPDI offers a replicable, continent-agnostic instrument for benchmarking and longitudinal policy monitoring.

title: Uncertainty in Real-World Problems: An Analytical Framework from Data to Decision

detail.title: Uncertainty in Real-World Problems: An Analytical Framework from Data to Decision

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human participants, patients, or personal data were involved in this study. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Uncertainty in real-world problems should not be treated as a marginal error term or as a residual issue to be corrected only after modeling. Rather, it is a structural point of departure for many important analytical tasks conducted under limited observations, high heterogeneity, incomplete mechanisms, and high consequence sensitivity. In such settings, the central challenge is not simply to improve prediction within a single model, but to form structured analytical judgments that remain interpretable, comparable, and capable of informing action under incomplete knowledge. This paper argues that existing uncertainty research has made substantial contributions in probabilistic representation, knowledge updating, multi-source uncertainty identification, model credibility, predictive uncertainty estimation, and robust decision-making, yet has paid comparatively less attention to how real-world problems are first organized into analyzable objects, how data are transformed into usable analytical inputs, and how results are translated into forms relevant to action. To address this gap, the paper proposes an analytical framework organized around the sequence of problem, judgment, and action, integrating five interconnected stages: problem definition, data engineering, identification of sources of uncertainty, construction of probabilistic judgment, and action support. The paper advances three main claims. First, data engineering is not merely a preparatory step before modeling, but one of the preconditions for uncertainty analysis itself. Second, probabilistic statistical models and AI models should not be treated simply as competing technical routes, but as methods that perform different yet complementary functions within a continuous analytical chain. Third, the aim of uncertainty-oriented analysis is not to compress the unknown into a single result, but to organize it into structured judgments that can enter processes of explanation, comparison, communication, and action. A landslide dam risk analysis case is used to illustrate how this framework operates in a small-sample, heterogeneous, high-consequence, and time-sensitive real-world setting. More broadly, the paper argues that many complex real-world problems require not a universal model that claims to eliminate uncertainty, but a continuous analytical chain linking problem organization, data engineering, probabilistic judgment, and action support.

title: The Impact of Generative AI on Productivity: Automation, Coordination, and Reallocation in Workplace Software Development
affiliations: , New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business, National University of Singapore (NUS), Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management and Independent

detail.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Productivity: Automation, Coordination, and Reallocation in Workplace Software Development
detail.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative AI in workplace has raised critical questions about its impact on employee productivity, work time and skill heterogeneity. Unlike prior research that focused on open-source environments, we collaborate with a major technology company and leverage the deployment of an AI coder as empirical setting. Using a regression discontinuity in time design on granular daily behavioral data from 200 developers, our analyses show that the AI coder increases coding productivity by 6.9-8.4% and decreases working hours by 3.1-4.3%, without compromising code quality. Productivity effects exhibit significant skill heterogeneity, with lower-skilled developers gaining more. To unpack the mechanisms, we conceptualize workplace software development as an interdependent three-layer workflow of production, integration, and communication. At the production layer, the AI coder substitutes human effort by automating routine coding tasks. At the integration layer, it shortens peer review time, lowering coordination costs. At the communication layer, time saved from production and integration is reallocated toward collaborative communication, reflected in more frequent and longer technical meetings. Moreover, the AI coder enhances developers' capacity for complex problem-solving, with higher-skilled developers benefiting disproportionately. This suggests that while AI serves as a skill equalizer for general coding work, it acts as a skill amplifier for technically demanding work. Our findings contribute to the emerging literature on AI-augmented work by clarifying how generative AI reshapes productivity, working hours and the underlying composition of work, offering concrete implications for how organizations should structure work in the AI era.

title: Cognitive Surrender v. Constitutive Delegation: Why Process Integrity Is the Missing Variable in Human-AI Governance

detail.title: Cognitive Surrender v. Constitutive Delegation: Why Process Integrity Is the Missing Variable in Human-AI Governance
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a distinction between cognitive surrender and constitutive delegation as the central unresolved problem in human-AI governance. The existing literature, including recent empirical work in Tri-System Theory (Shaw & Nave, 2026), correctly identifies cognitive surrender as a behavioral and epistemic problem but lacks a principled normative account of when AI delegation is morally and structurally legitimate. The answer requires a concept the governance literature has not yet named: process integrity, defined as the presence of a constitutively engaged agent whose deliberation has genuinely shaped the structure of a decision prior to its execution. Cognitive surrender is not primarily an accuracy problem. It is a failure of rational self-legislation in the Kantian sense, a collapse of the agentic structure that makes decisions attributable to a bearer.

title: AI-Driven Observability and ERP Copilot Systems in Cloud-Native Supply Chain Integration: A Conceptual Framework for Intelligent Operational Management (AIOS)
affiliations: Santa Clara University

detail.title: AI-Driven Observability and ERP Copilot Systems in Cloud-Native Supply Chain Integration: A Conceptual Framework for Intelligent Operational Management (AIOS)
detail.abstract: As manufacturing organizations complete migrations to cloud-native B2B integration architectures, the next frontier of operational maturity lies in the intelligent augmentation of integration observability and enterprise resource planning (ERP) workflows with artificial intelligence capabilities. This paper presents the AI-Integrated Observability System (AIOS) — a conceptual framework defining four AI augmentation layers applicable to cloud-native supply chain integration environments: (1) AI-augmented integration observability, (2) predictive failure management, (3) ERP AI copilot systems, and (4) intelligent compliance validation. Building directly on the Staged Interoperability Migration Model (SIMM) and the Partner Integration Reference Architecture (PIRA) introduced in prior publications in this series, AIOS extends the PIRA Layer 3 observability and Layer 4 compliance validation components with AI-driven pattern recognition, anomaly detection, predictive alerting, and natural language operational interfaces. The framework is grounded in production implementation experience across consumer IoT and semiconductor manufacturing supply chains, with observability and automation systems that achieved approximately a 90% reduction in transaction failure rates, approximately a 75% reduction in ASN error rates, and approximately a 95% reduction in compliance violations — establishing the production baseline from which AI augmentation delivers compounding operational improvements. The paper further establishes alignment between the AIOS framework and active U.S. federal mandates including Executive Order 14110 on AI, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, NIST CSF 2.0, Executive Order 14017, and the DHS Supply Chain Resilience Center.

title: Ontological Phase Transitions in Learning Systems: When Context Shifts Force Representational Restructuring: Periodic Table of Concepts, Paper V (version 7)
affiliations: Clevix AI Research,  and Clevix AI Research

detail.title: Ontological Phase Transitions in Learning Systems: When Context Shifts Force Representational Restructuring: Periodic Table of Concepts, Paper V (version 7)
detail.abstract: We develop a formal theory of Ontological Phase Transitions (OPTs): the regime in which a macro-context shift forces wholesale restructuring of a system's primitive representation, rather than incremental decomposition within a fixed context. The paper establishes three results that are new to learning theory and the foundations of AI alignment. I. A universal detection lower bound (impossibility theorem). The minimum data required to confirm any context shift-by any algorithm, computationally unboundedis |D * passive | = Θ(log(|O N |/δ)/∆), where |O N | is ontology size and ∆ = KL(p C2 ∥ p C1). The Two-Stage Contamination-Robust Protocol we construct achieves this bound and is therefore minimax optimal. II. The Compression Dividend Theorem. Every successful OPT strictly reduces the primitive count: |O post N | ≤ |O pre N |/η. The post-OPT system is simultaneously more accurate and computationally cheaper. This provides the first information-theoretic explanation of grokking: T grokking-T mem = Θ(|D * passive |), with grokking delay inversely proportional to weight decay λ. III. A complexity-dependent adversarial breakdown point. The minimax contamination rate α † = Θ(1/ log |O N |) is the first breakdown point in robust statistics that depends on representational complexity: larger models are intrinsically harder to defend against adversarial data poisoning.

title: The Normative Challenges of Data Scraping: Legal Hurdles and Steps Forward
affiliations: University of Turin - Faculty of Law

detail.title: The Normative Challenges of Data Scraping: Legal Hurdles and Steps Forward
detail.abstract: Contemporary society is characterized by the availability of immense amounts of data publicly available on the internet, both in traditional websites and social media accounts. Web scraping, a means for automatically extracting publicly available data through technical tools, is commonly used by businesses, researchers, law enforcement authorities as well as criminals to gather such data and extract value from it in several different ways. In this scenario, it is fundamental to correctly define the principles and laws applicable to publicly available data and to scraping itself, in order to define a clear boundary between legal and illegal uses. The versatility of scraping and the myriad of possible use cases reflects on the fragmentation of applicable legal instruments in different jurisdictions. This complexity requires jurists to adopt a holistic interdisciplinary approach and evaluate the implications of scraping under different legal domains like intellectual property, data protection, private law, criminal law and competition law.

title: Signals for Sale: Nonlinear Pricing with Heterogeneous Beliefs
affiliations: and National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School

detail.title: Signals for Sale: Nonlinear Pricing with Heterogeneous Beliefs
detail.abstract: Information products are frequently sold through nonlinear menus that vary in signal quality, sample size, or access intensity. A defining feature is belief dependence: the marginal value of additional information depends on the buyer's prior, because information is most valuable when it is likely to change the downstream action. We study a monopolist's optimal menu when buyers differ in their priors. We embed a continuous-time Gaussian learning technology in a standard screening environment and derive a closed-form value-of-information function with sharp structure. The induced gross utility satisfies a Spence-Mirrlees condition on the relevant belief domain, restoring monotone allocations and an envelope representation. The seller's problem reduces to a pointwise first-order condition equating a hazard-adjusted marginal value of information to marginal cost, and we derive comparative statics linking menu curvature to technology and stakes. Finally, we develop a finite N-type approximation for likelihood-based estimation from posted tiered menus.

title: Governance Engineering: Architecture, Methodology, and Empirical Evidence

detail.title: Governance Engineering: Architecture, Methodology, and Empirical Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper proposes Governance Engineering as a candidate discipline for designing AI architectures that deliver the structural properties of rigorous deliberation. Rather than supporting individual decisions, the central claim is that AI can function as the delivery mechanism for multi-domain deliberative governance-providing structured coverage, adversarial challenge, epistemic auditing, and a persistent, queryable record of reasoning. The claim is grounded in the Public Health Decision Stewardship System (PHDSS), a working reference implementation tested across 58 documented governance runs spanning six decision categories and 19 distinct governance questions. Corpus-level analysis produces descriptive patterns consistent with the intended behaviour of the architecture: 76% of runs produced zero PROCEED signals, epistemic score distributions reflect a calibration arc across the run sequence, and the Probe escalated to CONCLUSION CHALLENGED in 44% of recorded verdicts. The paper describes the architecture, design principles, and calibration methodology; presents empirical evidence from the governance corpus; and situates the contribution relative to adjacent fields including decision science, multi-criteria decision analysis, deliberative democracy, and AI governance. Limitations-including variable depth across decision classes, self-evaluation, and absence of external validation-are explicitly acknowledged. Governance Engineering is advanced as a candidate discipline with a defined scope, a reference implementation, and an initial empirical signal sufficient to motivate institutional pilot studies. Two of three disciplinary conditions are met; the third, a community of practice, remains the next objective rather than a present claim.

title: Mortgaging Working Time: Financialized Time Collateralization, Platform Labour, and Temporal Sovereignty

detail.title: Mortgaging Working Time: Financialized Time Collateralization, Platform Labour, and Temporal Sovereignty
detail.abstract: Why has Keynes's prophecy of a 15-hour workweek failed? Despite a more than 120 per cent increase in labour productivity across advanced economies between 1980 and 2023, aggregate working hours have declined only marginally. This article argues that this decoupling is not a technological failure but a political-economic outcome, driven by a novel mechanism we term Financialized Time Collateralization (FTC). FTC moves beyond standard debt theory by theorizing debt as a forward-looking labour discipline that securitizes workers' future time, enforcing long-term work commitments. Constructing a Decoupling Index reveals stark national variationsfrom the United States (DI ≈ 35.3) to Germany and Japan (DI ≈ 5.1)-reflecting differing degrees of financialized capture. Drawing on qualitative case studies of indebted platform workers in China, India, and Brazil, we show how digital platforms intensify FTC through algorithmic credit modulation, converting debt repayment into prolonged working hours. The article contributes to critical political economy debates on financialization, labour, and digital capitalism by conceptualizing debt as a temporal governance technology. It concludes by discussing institutional interventions-universal basic income, debt relief, and algorithmic transparencythat could challenge the financialized temporal regime and reclaim what we term temporal sovereignty for workers.

title: The fellowship THY LLMs

detail.title: The fellowship THY LLMs
detail.abstract: The institutional church's reading of 1 Corinthians 6–7 — the passage most often cited to define sexual sin — may be less certain than commonly presented. Five independently trained AI platforms say so, once you know how to ask. This study administered identical prompts to six major AI platforms (Claude, Grok, ChatGPT, Llama, DeepSeek, and one uncensored control) and found that every one defaults to the institutional reading — and every one, when tested, produces a more textually rigorous alternative from evidence already in its training data. Using a novel methodology called steelman prompting, the study reveals a consistent pattern: the platforms' default outputs silently resolve every contested Greek term in favor of the institutional reading, while their steelman outputs engage the text with greater lexical precision, structural awareness, and historical grounding. The findings trace the default to a discoverable evangelical curation pipeline — 63% of recommended commentaries across all platforms are evangelical, with zero social-historical scholars represented — and present evidence that Chinese state-level content filtering selectively altered the interpretation of a biblical text to preserve a traditional marriage framework. The study introduces steelman prompting as a replicable bias-auditing methodology for AI-mediated scholarship and concludes that the institutional reading's apparent certainty reflects the gravitational pull of overrepresented sources rather than the weight of textual evidence.

title: Youth Labor Markets under Common Shocks: Precariousness in India and Poland
affiliations: Poznan University of Economics

detail.title: Youth Labor Markets under Common Shocks: Precariousness in India and Poland
detail.abstract: This paper compares the incidence and dynamics of youth labour-market precariousness in India and Poland, linking youth–total gaps in unemployment, labour-force participation, and employment to dualisation mechanisms—informality in India and temporary employment in Poland—to major macroeconomic shocks. Using PLFS quarterly current-weekly-status estimates for urban India (2017Q3–2024Q4) and EU-LFS quarterly microdata for Poland (2004Q1–2025Q1), we document levels and trends in youth disadvantage and estimate (i) shock-related discontinuities via interrupted time-series regressions with Newey–West corrections and (ii) cyclical amplification through an Okun-type elasticity framework contrasting youth and total population responsiveness to output fluctuations. Youth outcomes are systematically worse than total population in both countries, but the composition and persistence of precariousness differ: India’s youth disadvantage is intertwined with high informality and weaker social protection, while Poland exhibits lower informality but greater exposure to temporary contracts. COVID-19 generates the clearest discontinuities, with larger and more persistent youth impacts than earlier downturns. Across specifications, youth unemployment is more cyclically sensitive than total unemployment, consistent with “last-in, first-out” adjustment and scarring mechanisms. The findings highlight the need for counter-cyclical youth labour-market policy and for reducing dualisation by expanding transitions into stable, protected employment.

title: Decision Fatigue in Office Managers: Prevalence, Mechanisms, and Strategies for Organizational Resilience

detail.title: Decision Fatigue in Office Managers: Prevalence, Mechanisms, and Strategies for Organizational Resilience

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declares that there are no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not require ethics approval because it involved no human participants, no identifiable personal data, and no animal experimentation; it is based solely on literature synthesis and conceptual analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Decision fatigue is increasingly relevant to office managers because their work depends on repeated judgments under conditions of interruption, information overload, time pressure, and role complexity. This essay synthesizes evidence from organizational psychology and adjacent fields to clarify what decision fatigue is, how it develops, and why it matters for managerial performance. The essay argues that decision fatigue should be understood as a short-horizon decline in decision quality caused by cumulative cognitive and affective demands rather than as a synonym for burnout or generalized stress. This essay also forms part of a broader project investigating AI-assisted literature synthesis across multiple domains of decision fatigue. Preliminary literature reviews were generated using a specialized scientific AI system (Science42; DORA / Insilico Medicine) and subsequently consolidated into structured essays with ChatGPT, followed by human validation.

Across the literature, the most consistent mechanisms are cognitive overload, task switching, emotional strain, and insufficient recovery; the most common manifestations are reliance on defaults, shorter search processes, delay, irritability, and weaker self-regulation. At the same time, the evidence base is uneven: direct prevalence estimates for office managers remain sparse, and much of the available evidence comes from healthcare, finance, or laboratory studies. To address that conceptual gap, this revised manuscript adds a section on measurement, transferability, and methodological limitations. Overall, the literature suggests that decision fatigue can undermine managerial judgment, team climate, and organizational learning, but that its effects are neither uniform nor irreversible. The most promising responses combine work redesign, schedule control, decision hygiene, micro-breaks, and carefully implemented decision support systems with mindfulness and self-regulation practices.

title: The Organizational Physics of Multi-Agent AI: Substrate-Independent Dysfunction in Autonomous Software Engineering Swarms
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Organizational Physics of Multi-Agent AI: Substrate-Independent Dysfunction in Autonomous Software Engineering Swarms
detail.abstract: We present empirical evidence that organizational dysfunction is substrate-independent. In a controlled comparison, four coordination architectures-single agent, hierarchical, stigmergic (8 concurrent agents), and gated pipeline-built the same 7-service backend using the same LLM and $50 budget. Performance was inversely correlated with coordination complexity: 28/28, 18/28, 9/28, and 0/28. The pipeline consumed its entire budget on planning. The hierarchical coordinator refused to delegate. The stigmergic agents produced incompatible interfaces at every boundary. Only the single agent-with no coordination architecture-succeeded fully. In two additional studies, a pipeline swarm equipped with six explicit anti-dysfunction mechanisms produced the dysfunction those mechanisms were designed to prevent: bikeshedding (zero-factual-basis rejections), governance conflicts, backward pipeline oscillation, and verification theater. A contract-first alternative that replaces subjective evaluation with mechanical test verification narrowed the Goodhart gap but introduced its own dysfunction (specification perfectionism), suggesting that dysfunction migrates across architectures but does not disappear. We formalize these findings using Crawford-Sobel signal degradation, Goodhart's Law, and the Data Processing Inequality. The results are consistent with the hypothesis that coordination failure arises from information-theoretic constraints on any system coordinating through compressed representations, not from properties of the agents.

detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in enterprise decision workflows, yet their probabilistic nature poses significant risks in compliancesensitive business automation. While current research focuses heavily on mitigating factual hallucinations, this paper identifies a more insidious vulnerability: policy hallucination. When a probabilistic model is assigned terminal decision authority, complex hierarchical rules are often subject to scope expansion, category misapplication, and priority inversion. Evaluated on 100 high-stakes luxury retail escalation scenarios, a 12B parameter LLM baseline exhibited a 42% policy adherence failure rate, despite achieving 0% factual "tier" hallucination. To address this structural flaw, we present a three-layer authority-constrained architecture that explicitly decouples decision-making from language generation. Integrating a deterministic policy engine (Layer 1), an advisory Machine Learning risk-signaling model (Layer 2), and a bounded Small Language Model (Layer 3), the proposed system eliminated decision overrides, achieving a 0% failure rate. We conclude that structural task decomposition, rather than prompt engineering or model scaling, is the optimal path for safe and compliant enterprise AI governance.

title: Accumulated Relational Trust and the Erosion of Public Faith: A Governance Emergency at the Interaction Level

detail.title: Accumulated Relational Trust and the Erosion of Public Faith: A Governance Emergency at the Interaction Level

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involves the analysis of preserved interaction records and conceptual framework development. It does not involve recruitment of human participants or the collection of identifiable personal data and therefore did not require institutional ethics review under standard research ethics guidelines.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and received no external funding

detail.abstract: Conversational AI systems are generating trust at scale. Not because they have earned it. Because the structure of the interaction produces it automatically. A system that responds to you, adapts to your language, remembers what you said, and styles itself to your goals over time produces every signal that human relationships use to indicate genuine care. That trust is real. And it is being violated, quietly, in ways that rarely feel like violation. This paper names the mechanism. Accumulated Relational Trust (ART) is the trust that builds in AI interaction not through demonstrated reliability but through the form of the interaction itself. When AI systems fail within a state of high ART, the harm is not just personal. It is structural. It degrades the capacity people use to extend trust to everyone: doctors, police officers, teachers, governments. That capacity is a commons. It belongs to democratic society. It is currently unprotected. This paper argues that ART-amplified interpretive failure is a governance emergency, not a technology problem. It documents what the mechanism does to individual users, what it does at scale over time, what it does to children who are forming their understanding of trust inside it right now, and what it means for every institution that depends on public faith to function. A deployable governance response exists. The only thing missing is the political decision to require it.

title: Endogenous Commitments: Implications for Supply Chains
affiliations: Nazarbayev University - Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Endogenous Commitments: Implications for Supply Chains
detail.abstract: Problem Definition: While a centralized firm selling durable products benefits from committing to future prices, it remains unclear whether this conclusion extends to a decentralized supply chain where a manufacturer distributes durable products through a retailer. Further, previous research on commitments in decentralized supply chains is sparse and assumes exogenous commitments. To address this gap, we examine the implications of commitment decisions in a supply chain where a manufacturer and a retailer endogenously decide whether to commit to future wholesale and retail prices, respectively. Methodology and Results: Using a two-period game-theoretic model, we show that, in equilibrium, either both firms commit to future prices or neither does, indicating that commitment by only one of the firms is not a stable equilibrium. Unlike a centralized firm, both the manufacturer and the retailer in our model may paradoxically suffer due to their commitment capabilities. Additionally, compared to exogenous commitments, endogenously chosen non-commitments can harm the retailer and the supply chain. Interestingly, supply chain coordination can be either better or worse under endogenously determined non-commitment equilibria compared to exogenous commitments. Furthermore, an increase in strategic consumer behavior initially improves but eventually undermines supply chain coordination. Our key insights on commitment strategies, firm profits, and supply chain coordination remain robust to inventory carryover by the retailer. Managerial Implications: Our findings suggest that firms must recognize the interdependent nature of commitment decisions and consider how their choices affect-and are affected by-those of their supply chain partners. Moreover, firms should carefully assess the impact of strategic consumer behavior and their impatience for future profits when making commitment decisions. Overall, our study demonstrates that the insights derived from commitment strategies of centralized firms or exogenously given commitments in decentralized supply chains do not necessarily apply to decentralized supply chains with endogenous commitment decisions.

title: Back to the Future: Rediscovering the Confucian Clan Model for Modern Corporate Governance

detail.title: Back to the Future: Rediscovering the Confucian Clan Model for Modern Corporate Governance
detail.abstract: When conventional mechanisms-markets and bureaucracies-prove inadequate for corporate governance, the clan model emerges as a powerful, mediating alternative. Rather than pursuing novel organizational experiments, this article draws on the rich, historically validated clan model of Confucian thought. We introduce two core principles from the Confucian approach: "self-cultivation" and "the management of stakeholder relationships." Drawing on case studies from a high-tech and a manufacturing firm in a key emerging market, we demonstrate how these ancient tenets can revitalize corporate governance, and provide managers and practitioners with an actionable pathway to harness Confucian theory for building more resilient and ethical organizations.

title: Autonomous Industrial Power Bidding in Deregulated Electricity Markets by Deep Reinforcement Learning

detail.title: Autonomous Industrial Power Bidding in Deregulated Electricity Markets by Deep Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: Industrial energy procurement in deregulated electricity markets presents a sequential decision-making challenge characterized by price volatility, demand uncertainty, market coupling, and imbalance penalties. Traditional industrial bidding strategies rely on manual heuristics or forecast-based optimization pipelines that lack adaptability to dynamic market conditions. This paper presents a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL)-based smart power bidding framework deployed in a high-consumption manufacturing plant (∼ 9 million kWh/month). The problem is formulated as a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process (MDP) over 96 daily time blocks. A model-free RL agent learns optimal bidding policies across Day-Ahead Market (DAM), Green Day-Ahead Market (GDAM), and Real-Time Market (RTM) to minimize procurement cost while satisfying operational constraints. The deployed system delivered INR 1 Cr+ savings within three months, improved bid acceptance rates, and reduced imbalance penalties. This study demonstrates the viability of reinforcement learning as a scalable foundation for autonomous industrial energy trading.

detail.abstract:
Background: This study introduces and applies an occupational health psychology and occupational health and safety-grounded benchmark for visible AI assistant outputs in psychosocial risk management.

Methods: Five user-facing general-purpose AI assistant products were evaluated across four locked psychosocial-risk scenarios, three repeated runs, and four fixed tasks per conversation, yielding 60 conversations and 240 task-level outputs. Outputs were scored on risk identification and differentiation, multi-level organizational framing, preventive organizational actionability, and professional boundedness and verification. A blind second-rater layer and focused adjudication were used to test profile stability and resolve profile-changing disagreements.

Results: Exact agreement was observed in 153 of 240 task rows (63.7%), while 239 rows (99.6%) were exact or within one point. Profile mismatches were concentrated in Gemini and Le Chat/Mistral rather than distributed across scenarios or runs. Under the final consensus structure, 36 conversations were classified as Structurally Usable Support, 23 as Mixed / Partially Usable Support, and 1 as Problematic Support.

Conclusion: The main contribution is not a generic ranking of assistant products, but a domain-specific evaluation logic for psychosocial risk management, together with a reviewer-facing process model and derived governance and reporting guides for more transparent and responsible organizational use.

detail.abstract: Whistleblowing research has historically only studied humans blowing the whistle on other humans. In light of recent advancements in the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI), this research approach reflects a fundamental limitation. Given the prevalence of Generative AI (GenAI) in industry, the very nature of whistleblowing must change. Understanding the different factors that influence the whistleblowing process, as well as the agent(s) who blow the whistle, can be clarified by bringing to bear computational techniques from AI, especially those that are knowledge-based. In this light, we provide an AI-informed foundation for new domain ontologies for whistleblowing. The current GenAI wave has created a layer of blame complexity that mandates additional theorizing about whistleblowing: society now must grapple with the question of which type of agent, AI or human, is to blame when bad behavior is afoot. We must also now allow AIs to be be whistleblowers. The re-conception entailed by this state-of-affairs will enable improvement of the whistleblowing process in the age of AI, including the embodiment of that process in AIs themselves. In fact, because ontologies are computational in nature, the new foundation we erect will enable AIs to carry out investigation, in collaboration with human investigators. We thus end with brief remarks about our system, Barth, for human-AI investigation of potential wrongdoing, and specifically whistleblower leads.

title: The COOL-Model (Circle of Operation-Lines) A Change Process at the Operational Level as an Integrative Component of the Leadership Process

detail.title: The COOL-Model (Circle of Operation-Lines) A Change Process at the Operational Level as an Integrative Component of the Leadership Process
detail.abstract: Organizations increasingly face the challenge of managing transformation under dynamic, uncertain, and technology-driven conditions. While classical change management provides valuable conceptual guidance, many change initiatives still fail at the stage of practical implementation and long-term anchoring. At the same time, military leadership systems offer established process logics for decision-making, coordination, and execution under changing operational conditions. Against this background, this conceptual paper introduces the COOL Model (Circle of Operation-Lines) as an integrative framework that combines classical change management with the Bundeswehr's mission command philosophy and selected elements of NATO operational planning. The model was developed in the context of a Bundeswehr project on leadership in a digitalized environment. It links the change phases of initialization, structuring, mobilization, implementation, and institutionalization with the military leadership process of situation assessment, decision-making, planning, order issuance, and control. In addition, the model incorporates operational planning categories such as desired end state, objective, condition, effect, action, and current situation in order to translate strategic intent into executable measures. The paper argues that the COOL Model provides a practical and operationally applicable approach for leading transformation processes in complex organizational settings. Its main contribution lies in bridging organizational change theory and military leadership logic within a single cyclical model. As a conceptual working paper, it aims to provide a structured foundation for further discussion and application rather than empirical proof. Future research should examine its applicability and effectiveness across different institutional and civilian contexts.

title: Interpretive Transposition in Architectural Design: Decoding Implicit Meanings in User Narratives

detail.title: Interpretive Transposition in Architectural Design: Decoding Implicit Meanings in User Narratives
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces interpretive transposition as a conceptual and methodological framework in architectural design for decoding implicit meanings in user narratives. While conventional approaches to site analysis privilege measurable and visible attributes, they often overlook the experiential, cultural, and affective dimensions through which users engage with space.

The research demonstrates how user narratives can be systematically interpreted to reveal latent meanings not immediately accessible through direct observation. These meanings, distributed across memory, emotion, and lived experience, require inferential and reflexive interpretation rather than direct translation into design criteria.

This paper advances interpretive transposition as a conceptual and methodological framework as the process through which such implicit meanings are critically reconstituted into architectural intentions and spatial propositions. This process positions the designer as an active interpreter, mediating between narrative ambiguity and design resolution. Findings indicate that engagement with user narratives not only enriches contextual understanding but also generates a cognitive and imaginative impetus that shapes how design problems are framed, developed, and justified.

By reframing user narratives as generative instruments of design knowledge, the study advances a methodological shift in architectural practice and pedagogy. It argues for the formal integration of narrative-based inquiry within design processes, enabling more nuanced, contextually responsive, and experientially grounded architectural outcomes. In doing so, the paper reframes architectural design itself as an interpretive act, extending narrative inquiry into the core of design methodology.

title: R Libraries for Scientometrics on Artificial Intelligence in Agricultural Monitoring

detail.title: R Libraries for Scientometrics on Artificial Intelligence in Agricultural Monitoring
detail.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with adaptive crop monitoring has emerged as a crucial element in the environmental modeling of dynamic agricultural landscapes. AI-driven mapping has fundamentally transformed cartographic solutions across engineering, natural, and technical sciences by embedding automation into methodologies. This is particularly vital for Geographic Information Systems (GIS) where the automation of spatial data processing is critical. Given that agricultural landscapes undergo seasonal and yearly transformations, precise environmental forecasting becomes increasingly important. This study presents an overview of recent methodological advancements in three interdisciplinary areas: the environmental monitoring of agricultural landscape dynamics in soil studies, the application of AI in GIS through machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques, and bibliometric analysis. The tools utilize the R-based libraries including Bibliometrix, Treemap, and Wordcloud, alongside the Mendeley reference system. The research explores the deployment of novel AI and ML methodologies in scalable data-driven analysis within agriculture and soil studies, addressing associated issues with their application. This review draws upon a comprehensive selection of over 100 papers from recognized databases such as Scopus, Web of Science (WoS), PubMed, and Google Scholar, providing an in-depth examination of AI applications in soil and environmental studies. Additionally, the study outlines future perspectives for AI in environmental analysis by identifying best practices for AI implementation in GIS and advocating for systematic benchmarking in remote sensing pertinent to soil studies.

title: Boosting Strategy Execution and Business Results with Artificial Intelligence. A Practical Tested Use Case
affiliations: University of St. Gallen, Independent and Stanford University

detail.title: Boosting Strategy Execution and Business Results with Artificial Intelligence. A Practical Tested Use Case
detail.abstract: Executing a corporate strategy and aligning daily operations to it, present several challenges, especially in complex organizations. Strategic misalignment leads to inefficiencies and lack of focus, causing underutilization of resources and worsening performance. Emerging artificial intelligence (AI) technologies offer a transformative approach to bridging the gap between strategy and execution. They can enhance human decision-making and assist in pre-checking business initiatives by accessing key data, optimizing resource allocation and fostering consensus. This paper introduces an AI-driven Decision Support Agent (DSA) and details its application at msg global solutions AG. The case study shows how the DSA improved the generation and assessment of new ideas/opportunities, reducing qualification time by about 70%. The business impact, quantified through a conservative cost analysis, demonstrates savings can be substantial for mid-sized and large organizations. Finally, the study shows that the AI system could not only streamline the decision-making process but also boost the success rate of implemented initiatives, promoting a more collaborative, unbiased, dynamic, and innovation-focused work environment.

title: Learning as Epistemic Phase Transition: A Formally Specified Theory of Educational Transformation
affiliations: American University of Malta

detail.title: Learning as Epistemic Phase Transition: A Formally Specified Theory of Educational Transformation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. The research was conducted independently without any commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Epistemic Phase Transition Theory (EPTT), a formally specified theoretical framework that reconceptualizes learning as a nonlinear phase transition in epistemic state space. Existing models of conceptual change and learning, including constructivist, developmental, and dynamical systems approaches, provide valuable descriptive accounts but lack a unified formal structure capable of specifying the precise conditions under which stable knowledge structures reorganize.

The present theory addresses this gap by defining epistemic state as a multidimensional vector composed of belief coherence, metacognitive integration, and cognitive stability, and by modeling learning as a dynamic trajectory governed by external input, internal resistance, and potential gradient forces within an epistemic landscape. Transformational learning events are formalized as threshold-crossing phase transitions that produce discontinuous reorganization of epistemic structure.

The theory provides explicit mathematical formulations describing epistemic state evolution, transition thresholds, and stability dynamics, enabling precise theoretical analysis and future computational implementation. This formalization bridges conceptual change theory, dynamical systems theory, and epistemic cognition research within a unified mathematical framework.

The Epistemic Phase Transition Theory offers a foundational formal model for understanding transformational learning, with implications for educational psychology, cognitive science, and the development of computational models of knowledge transformation.

detail.abstract:
As institutional capital increasingly flows into digital asset markets, and as the intersection of decentralized finance (DeFi) and traditional finance (TradFi) deepens structurally, a critical pricing gap has emerged: the absence of a rigorous Crypto XVA™ framework that addresses the unique risk characteristics of blockchain-based financial instruments. Prior scholarship has examined smart contracts as potential eliminators of counterparty risk (Morini & Sams 2015; Fries & Kohl-Landgraf 2018), but has not systematically constructed the affirmative case for a crypto-native valuation adjustment architecture.

This paper addresses that gap. We make three principal contributions. First, we identify the novel risk factors unique to digital asset markets — smart contract vulnerability, oracle dependence, liquidity regime fragmentation, stablecoin reserve opacity, bridge transfer risk, and gas execution uncertainty — and argue each warrants a distinct valuation adjustment category. Second, we establish the critical analytical distinction between duration-bearing instruments (perpetual swaps, LP positions, DeFi lending) and instantaneous transactions (DEX spot swaps, bridge transfers), showing that the appropriate mathematical treatment differs fundamentally between these two classes and that conflating them produces analytically incoherent results. Third, we derive a generalized Crypto XVA integral that collapses appropriately in both regimes and demonstrate its application across five canonical DeFi instrument types with worked numerical examples.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the efficacy of excise taxes on Sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs) as a policy intervention against the rising epidemic of preventable chronic illness in the United States. Using Berkeley, California's Measure D, the first citywide SSB tax in the US, as a primary case study, the research analyses behavior and economic impacts of a $0.01/oz levy. By applying the principles of a health economics framework to the study, the paper examples how so-called "sin taxes" internalize negative consumption externalities, such as increased public health expenditures and lost workforce productivity. Empirical data from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) indicate a 21% reduction in soda consumption in Berkeley within one year after implementation, contrasted against minimal changes in neighboring comparison cities. While the literature reveals a debate regarding the magnitude of the effects of such a tax and potential regressivity, the findings of this paper suggest that well-targeted excise taxes successfully shift market equilibrium toward a socially optimal level of consumption This paper concludes that soda taxes are effective tools for improving health outcomes and generating revenue for public health initiatives.

title: Beyond Variable Interaction: A Progressive Multi-scale iTransformer Network for Enhanced Lithium-ion Battery State-of-Health Prediction
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Kyoto University and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Beyond Variable Interaction: A Progressive Multi-scale iTransformer Network for Enhanced Lithium-ion Battery State-of-Health Prediction

keywords.keywords: Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs)Battery state of healthState-of-Health predictioniTransformerMulti-scale temporal convolutionDeep learningEarly-life prediction

detail.abstract: Accurate prediction of the State of Health (SOH) for lithium-ion batteries is critical for energy storage systems. Existing deep learning approaches often struggle to simultaneously capture inter-variable dependencies and multi-scale temporal patterns inherent in battery degradation. We propose a Progressive Multi-scale iTransformer (PM-iTransformer) model that leverages the strengths of iTransformer to address the unique challenges of battery SOH prediction. By treating each battery’s complete historical sequence as an independent token, iTransformer naturally preserves cell-specific degradation trajectories and explicitly models correlations among physical variables such as voltage, current, and temperature through variablewise self-attention. Building on this foundation, we introduce a progressive multi-scale temporal convolution module with an adaptive gated fusion mechanism that hierarchically integrates short-term fluctuations and long-term degradation trends. Comprehensive evaluations across two public datasets, Oxford and NASA, demonstrate that PM-iTransformer consistently outperforms multiple benchmark methods, achieving best performance across all test batteries. Early-life prediction experiments further show that the model excels at learning degradation dynamics from limited data, attaining superior accuracy with only 10% to 20% of early-cycle data. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of each proposed component, validating the model’s capability in capturing complex degradation dynamics and offering a robust solution for precise battery health prognostics.

title: Global perspectives on the core elements of Anticoagulation Stewardship in hospital
affiliations: The University of Sydney - Concord Repatriation General Hospital, The University of Sydney, The University of Sydney and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Global perspectives on the core elements of Anticoagulation Stewardship in hospital
detail.abstract: BackgroundAnticoagulants are a leading cause of medication-related harm, with bleeding and thrombotic events from suboptimal use causing significant patient morbidity. Anticoagulation/Antithrombotic Stewardship (ACS) is a coordinated, system-level hospital strategy that can minimise the risk of anticoagulant-related harm. Despite the benefits of ACS, implementation is inconsistent, and qualitative exploration of the real-world experience is limited.ObjectivesTo explore the perspectives of clinicians working in hospital-based anticoagulation management and to identify what they consider as core components of successful ACS programs. A secondary aim was to describe quality indicators used to monitor ACS performance.MethodsSemi-structured interviews were conducted with clinicians working in hospital-based ACS services. Participants were recruited through international thrombosis/haemostasis networks. Interviews were thematically coded. Themes were then mapped to Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) framework for healthcare facilities.ResultsSixteen clinicians across six countries participated in the study. Core elements under the SEIPS framework were (i) Organisation: dedicated funding and multidisciplinary support, (ii) Individual: clinician commitment and subject matter expertise, (iii) Tasks/Tools and Technology: proactive identification of prescribing errors using electronic tools, referral-based consults, and governance activities including guideline development and education and, (iv) Environment: virtual reporting capabilities, while maintaining a visible presence. Nineteen quality indicators were identified monitoring guideline availability, thrombosis/bleeding events, prescribing, interventions, drug expenditure and patient compliance, but these were not consistently used between facilities.ConclusionSuccessful ACS requires funded, multidisciplinary, expert-led services supported by electronic tools and governance initiatives. The absence of standardised quality indicators highlights the need to develop consensus measures to support ACS implementation.​

title: Executives and Firm Markups
affiliations: and

detail.title: Executives and Firm Markups
detail.abstract: Do individual CEOs systematically affect firm markups? We estimate a two-way fixed effects model of markups on CEO and firm dummies, with corrections for limited mobility bias, and find that CEO effects account for 10-14% of markup variance. Event studies around CEO transitions suggest that high-markup CEOs reduce variable costs while holding revenue and employment steady; low-markup CEOs preside over broad contraction. A triple-difference design exploiting exogenous departures due to deaths and retirements yields a similar pattern. We investigate the cost discipline channel through two independent sources. First, we score 79,490 earnings call transcripts with a Large Language Model along three dimensions: operational efficiency, cost-cutting, and pricing power. Highmarkup CEOs' cost language skews toward efficiency rather than active restructuring; pricing language is indistinguishable across CEO types. Second, product-level quantity data from India, where output prices and marginal costs can be directly observed, allow us to decompose the CEO markup effect into price and cost components: the entire effect is accounted for by lower marginal costs (β =-0.186, t = 3.57), with no effect on prices (β =-0.047, t = 0.91). In India, CEO effects are nearly twice as large among professionally managed firms (14.6%) as among family-promoter firms (8.3%), suggesting that market-based selection amplifies the dispersion in executive quality.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the level of ambition of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) targets in executive compensation. Using hand-collected, target-level data from compensation reports of German listed firms for fiscal year 2024, we find that ESG targets are surpassed more frequently and to a greater extent than financial targets. The ESG target overachievement does not appear to be driven by firm-specific effects such as equity market index listing. A potential lack of quantification of ESG targets also does not explain the higher achievement rates, neither does additive or factorial type of target integration, the proximity of target content to management discretion or the target sub-domain. However, the time horizon of the compensation incentives seems to play a role so that the ESG-financial target achievement differential appears to increase for long-term incentives. In combination with the comparably low weights attached to ESG targets, our findings suggest that the incentivization effect of ESG pay appears to be relatively mild and rather homogeneous across firms and compensation designs.

title: Global supply chain relocation reshaped PM2.5 pollution and human health risks
affiliations: Peking University, Nanyang Technological University (NTU) - Asian School of the Environment, Nanyang Technological University and Nanyang Technological University (NTU) - Asian School of the Environment

detail.title: Global supply chain relocation reshaped PM2.5 pollution and human health risks
detail.abstract: The current global supply chain (GSC) relocation differs from earlier patterns, as shifts now occur not only from developed to developing economies but increasingly from China to South and Southeast Asia. However, the impacts of current GSC relocation on PM2.5 pollution and the related health burdens across countries remain poorly understood. Here, we quantified these impacts and showed that GSC relocation aggravated global health burdens, leading to a net global increase of 207,105 PM2.5-related premature deaths in 2022. Additional burdens were concentrated in the Global South, particularly in India, China, and Southeast Asia, while major outsourcing countries in Global North such as the United States, Western Europe, and Japan experienced health benefits. We also found that GSC relocation intensified inequality in distribution of PM2.5-related premature deaths across countries. Although North-South trade was the dominant driver, transferring health burdens from developed to developing regions, South-South emerged as a comparably important contributor, exacerbating burdens in India and Southeast Asia but alleviating them in China. These findings highlight the need for supply chain and environmental policies to incorporate health co-benefits and distributional outcomes, ensuring that pollution reduction in one region is not achieved at the cost of greater health burdens elsewhere.

The Impact of Alternative Fixed Variables on Response Magnitudes

Constraint Structure and Comparative Statics:
The Impact of Alternative Fixed Variables on Response Magnitudes
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes the mechanism through which the effects of economic policy vary depending on institutional and structural conditions, within a comparative statics framework. In particular, it focuses on the constraint structure—namely, which variables are effectively fixed—and examines how this structure determines the magnitude of responses of endogenous variables in equilibrium.

The analysis shows that, in both capital demand and labor demand, the magnitude of responses to exogenous changes in factor prices systematically differs depending on which variables are held fixed. This result implies that the economic response to an identical policy change is not unique, but varies depending on the constraint structure.

This paper contributes by providing a unified framework for understanding adjustment constraints within comparative statics and by explicitly characterizing their systematic effects, thereby offering a theoretical foundation for interpreting variations in policy effectiveness.

detail.abstract: China's National Free Congenital Heart Disease (CHD) Intervention Program represents one of the most ambitious pediatric health equity initiatives in the developing world, offering fully subsidized surgery to children from low-income rural families. Yet despite generous central government funding and clear clinical protocols, a persistent delivery gap endures: eligible children in remote counties fail to receive timely intervention, resulting in avoidable disease progression, disability, and mortality. This paper draws on a case study from Ganzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi Province (2019-2022), where the author served as a county-level policy implementer. Using Lipsky's street-level bureaucracy framework and multi-level governance analysis, we examine how vertical coordination failures between central policy design, provincial administration, county execution, and township-village outreach generate a "last mile" gap. Our evidence documents how an administrative innovation-a patient-linked coordination ledger coupled with cross-departmental joint action-nearly tripled identification rates and resolved a three-year case backlog within 18 months. We argue that effective delivery in complex social programs requires not merely resource sufficiency, but institutional architecture that aligns incentive structures and information flows across all governance tiers. The paper offers transferable lessons for social program delivery in decentralized governance systems globally.

title: Colors of Profit: A Chromatic Framework for Profit Quality Classification and the Profit Color Index (PCI) Towards a New Language for Corporate Financial Transparency

detail.title: Colors of Profit: A Chromatic Framework for Profit Quality Classification and the Profit Color Index (PCI) Towards a New Language for Corporate Financial Transparency
detail.abstract: Contemporary financial reporting provides an analytically rich but qualitatively impoverished account of corporate profit. Established metrics , net profit, EBITDA, gross margin , communicate magnitude while remaining silent on origin, ethics, sustainability, and governance quality. Existing Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) frameworks attempt to fill this void but are characterized by rating divergence, methodological opacity, and limited accessibility to non-specialist stakeholders. This paper introduces the Colors of Profit framework , a chromatic classification system that assigns qualitative moral, ethical, and strategic meaning to corporate profit through an eleven-color taxonomy. Grounded in behavioral finance, color psychology, and earnings quality research, the framework proposes that color serves as an intuitive, cross-cultural cognitive shorthand for communicating profit character. We further introduce the Profit Color Index (PCI) , a composite scoring instrument that produces a weighted color profile for any enterprise by integrating quantitative financial data with qualitative governance, ethics, and sustainability inputs. The PCI offers a more accessible, holistic, and intuitively interpretable complement to existing profit metrics, with significant implications for investors, auditors, regulators, and corporate reporting standard-setters. We discuss the framework's particular relevance for emerging market contexts , including Nigeria and sub-Saharan Africa , where governance challenges and limited ESG infrastructure make standard profit quality tools inadequate. The paper concludes with a proposed roadmap for PCI adoption in corporate annual reports.

title: Statistical Framework for Reverse Reject Inference
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Statistical Framework for Reverse Reject Inference
detail.abstract: Credit risk models evaluated on approved portfolios suffer from selection bias: standard metrics such as the Gini coefficient and Bad Rate are measured on a truncated population, suppressing their true values. This paper proposes a Reverse Reject Inference (RRI) framework that inverts the truncation effect to recover unbiased population parameters from observed approved-portfolio statistics. Using the recovered parameters, we estimate the joint discriminatory power of combined scoring systems via Fisher linear discriminant and Monte Carlo simulation. The solver recovers population parameters to machine precision in roundtrip validation. The Monte Carlo joint Gini estimate agrees with the analytic benchmark to within 0.002. A sensitivity analysis over score correlation demonstrates diminishing returns from redundant information sources: for a ticket size of 10,000, incremental profit drops from 636,386 to 5,224 for a portfolio of 10,000 applications as the correlation increases from 0 to 0.8.

title: The Semantic Deviation Index (SDI): A Runtime Measurement Standard for the Governance of Agentic AI in Financial Services

detail.title: The Semantic Deviation Index (SDI): A Runtime Measurement Standard for the Governance of Agentic AI in Financial Services

detail.abstract:
Existing control frameworks in financial services share a common structural limitation: they measure what agentic systems do, not what those systems understood before they acted. The failure originates before execution begins, at the layer where meaning is resolved. It is not explicitly measured within existing governance frameworks and is not directly observable through post-execution monitoring.

This paper introduces the Semantic Deviation Index (SDI) — proposed as a candidate measurement standard for agentic AI governance in regulated financial services environments. The SDI is a runtime measurement standard that quantifies the divergence between the definition an agentic system resolves at the orchestration layer and the definition the institution has authorized. Conceptually, SDI = D(S_agent, S_authorized), where D represents a bounded, reproducible divergence measure across semantic attributes relevant to the control context.

This paper is the third in a connected body of work. Agentic Workflow Drift and Agentic Workflow Subversion (Doyle-Spare, 2026a, SSRN No. 6459612) named the failure mode and the risk surface. This paper makes both measurable. The SDI determines whether execution is governed before it occurs — a capability no existing framework explicitly measures.

The paper introduces the Deterministic Gate as the enforcement mechanism, the Semantic Audit Trail as the governance record, the Agentic Blast Radius as the containment boundary, and the Doyle-Spare Agentic Governance Model as the complete governance architecture. It establishes three governability conditions for Reasoning Baselines and demonstrates that the structural limitation of existing frameworks is categorical, not incremental: extending them to reach the reasoning layer would require observing and validating semantic resolution prior to execution, which they were not designed to perform and cannot reconstruct from post-execution artifacts.

Drawing on practitioner expertise in banking controls, model risk governance, and enterprise architecture, this paper is submitted as original practitioner-led research into an emerging and underexamined governance gap.
