Part III provides Python and R code skeletons for data ingestion, normalization, model estimation, and the full 10-step validation workflow. All materials are designed for direct use by independent research teams executing the SVA blind retrospective validation study.

title: Digital Economy Impacts through the Lens of Leontief and Miyazawa Multipliers: Evidence from Vietnam’s 2012, 2019, and 2024 Input-Output Tables.
affiliations: and National Statistical Office

detail.title: Digital Economy Impacts through the Lens of Leontief and Miyazawa Multipliers: Evidence from Vietnam’s 2012, 2019, and 2024 Input-Output Tables.
detail.abstract:
This paper analyzes the role and spillover mechanisms of the digital economy in Vietnam from 2012 to 2024 using Input-Output (I-O) tables. By employing both the traditional Leontief model and the Miyazawa demographic-economic model (DEM), the study compares output and value-added multipliers to evaluate the scale and quality of effects.

 The results indicate that the value-added share of the digital economy in GDP, when accounted for within the DEM, reached approximately 19.6% by 2024, reflecting its increasing importance in the national growth model. Meanwhile, under the traditional Leontief model, the digital economy's value-added share of GDP was only about 8.7% in 2024. Although the Miyazawa multipliers remain significantly higher than the Leontief ones, they show a narrowing gap over time. This trend suggests a decline in the efficiency of the income-consumption-production - redistribution loop diffusion mechanism, primarily due to heavy reliance on imports and Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). 

The study emphasizes that expanding the digital economy must be accompanied by policies to enhance domestic value-added and improve income distribution mechanisms to maximize spillover effects, thereby supporting sustainable digital economic development.

detail.abstract:
This paper advances a formal architectural interpretation of ecclesial organization, articulating what is termed the Ecclesiastical Consensus Principle: the proposition that the Church, as described in the New Testament, functions as a Spirit-anchored distributed network in which authority is unified in Christ, capability is distributed across participants, and coherence is sustained through alignment rather than centralization.

Drawing from scriptural exegesis and systems architecture theory, the study reframes foundational ecclesiological constructs—Pentecost, spiritual gifts, the Body of Christ, and apostolic teaching—as elements of a coherent distributed system. Within this framework, no individual participant or local congregation embodies complete functional sufficiency; rather, the full expression of the Church emerges through coordinated participation across interdependent members. This distributed configuration is shown to generate emergent properties, including cooperation, unity, and humility, which are not merely moral exhortations but structural outcomes of the system’s design.

The paper further demonstrates that ecclesial authority, while singular in source, is non-concentrated in function. By preventing the consolidation of complete operational capability within any single human agent, the architecture of the Church exhibits a form of structural constraint analogous to anti-concentration principles in legal and institutional design. This configuration reduces systemic vulnerability, resists domination, and preserves continuity across time without reliance on centralized enforcement mechanisms.

Particular attention is given to the role of gathering as a synchronization mechanism within the distributed network, through which alignment is periodically reinforced, and to the emergence of humility as a necessary condition for system stability, especially as responsibility increases within the body. In this respect, the study advances the claim that ecclesiastical humility is not solely a normative virtue but a functional requirement inherent to the structure of the system itself.

This analysis does not propose a revision to established doctrine but offers a structural clarification of patterns already present within the New Testament. By interpreting ecclesial organization through the lens of distributed systems, the paper provides a framework through which unity, authority, and participation may be understood as legally and structurally coherent within a non-centralized institutional model.

In doing so, the study contributes to broader discussions in institutional theory, governance, and
legal architecture by demonstrating that durable systems of authority may be designed to
preserve coherence without centralization, and that constraints on power concentration may be
embedded not only through regulation, but through the underlying structure of the system itself.

title: Net Zero and Inflation Expectations: The Role of Monetary and Fiscal Policies
affiliations: University of Macau, , University of Birmingham and University of Birmingham

detail.title: Net Zero and Inflation Expectations: The Role of Monetary and Fiscal Policies
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the UK net zero transition on household inflation expectations using a randomized survey experiment with 2,451 UK participants. We identify the causal effects of net-zero transition scenarios and policies on inflation expectations over different horizons. Our results show that (1) tightening transition policy through a reduction in the cap of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) significantly raises 1-year-ahead inflation expectations, with the upward revision primarily driven through the increasing economic cost reasoning mechanism; (2) fiscal policy in the form of increasing green subsidies leads to a moderate increase in near-term inflation expectations, driven by both green investment and economic cost reasoning mechanism; and (3) clarifying the inflation target, as a form of central bank communication, significantly reduces inflation expectations across all horizons. Overall, both ETS cap reductions and green subsidies raise short-term inflation expectations while clear central bank communication can effectively manage the inflation expectations through anchoring mechanism.

title: Matters Arising from: Official Estimates of Global Food Insecurity Undercount Acute Hunger
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, , affiliation not provided to SSRN, Independant researcher and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Matters Arising from: Official Estimates of Global Food Insecurity Undercount Acute Hunger

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial conflicts
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: No funding received

detail.abstract:
This comment examines the analysis presented in Lentz et al. (2025), which concludes that subnational food security assessments systematically underestimate the number of acutely food insecure people globally. We assess the two main components of their analysis: a comparison of Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) estimates to alternative counterfactuals, and a distributional analysis of IPC classifications around the Phase 3 (Crisis) threshold.

We argue that the counterfactual approaches employed are not sufficiently grounded in established food security measurement frameworks to support inferences about underestimation, and that the distributional analysis, while methodologically informative, implies only modest deviations that fall within the range of uncertainty typically associated with operational food security assessments. In addition, the concentration of observations in a small number of countries raises questions about the generalizability of global conclusions.

Taken together, these considerations suggest that the magnitude and direction of any systematic bias in current estimates of acute food insecurity remain uncertain. We outline areas where further analysis—particularly those leveraging household-level data and alternative counterfactual constructions—could provide a more robust basis for evaluating potential underestimation.

title: Delegation and Verification Under AI
affiliations: Nanjing University,  and Yale University

detail.title: Delegation and Verification Under AI
detail.abstract: As AI systems enter institutional workflows, workers must decide whether to delegate task execution to AI and how much effort to invest in verifying AI outputs, while institutions evaluate workers using outcome-based standards that may misalign with workers' private costs. We model delegation and verification as the solution to a rational worker's optimization problem, and define worker quality by evaluating an institution-centered utility (distinct from the worker's objective) at the resulting optimal action. We formally characterize optimal worker workflows and show that AI induces phase transitions, where arbitrarily small differences in verification ability lead to sharply different behaviors. As a result, AI can amplify workers with strong verification reliability while degrading institutional worker quality for others who rationally over-delegate and reduce oversight, even when baseline task success improves and no behavioral biases are present. These results identify a structural mechanism by which AI reshapes institutional worker quality and amplifies quality disparities between workers with different verification reliability.

title: Decomposing Loan Rate Dispersion in the Interbank Market
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University

detail.title: Decomposing Loan Rate Dispersion in the Interbank Market
detail.abstract: This paper decomposes loan rate dispersion in the interbank market. Using transactionlevel data, we document dispersion in uncollateralized overnight loan rates even during periods of low interest rates in Japan. Applying the AKM model, we quantify the contributions of borrower and lender heterogeneity to loan rate dispersion. Lender heterogeneity explains about three times more dispersion than borrower heterogeneity. The contribution of borrower heterogeneity declines over time. Positive assortative matching in borrowers' and lenders' average loan rates is observed. For term loans, borrower heterogeneity accounts for a larger share of loan rate dispersion than for overnight loans.

title: Digital Transformation in Banking: Navigating the Fintech Revolution, Cybersecurity Imperatives, and Regulatory Frontiers in the Global Digital Economy
affiliations: and Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics

detail.title: Digital Transformation in Banking: Navigating the Fintech Revolution, Cybersecurity Imperatives, and Regulatory Frontiers in the Global Digital Economy
detail.abstract: The global banking sector is undergoing a profound structural transformation driven by the rapid proliferation of digital technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, cloud computing, and mobile platforms. This policy paper examines the multidimensional implications of digital transformation in banking, focusing on the convergence of fintech innovation, evolving regulatory landscapes, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, and financial inclusion imperatives. Drawing on empirical data, comparative regulatory analysis, and sector-specific case studies from both advanced and emerging economies, the paper identifies key drivers, structural challenges, and strategic opportunities reshaping the contemporary banking ecosystem. The findings underscore that while digital transformation enhances operational efficiency, customer experience, and financial access, it simultaneously introduces systemic risks related to data privacy, third-party dependencies, and regulatory arbitrage. The paper argues that sustainable digital banking requires a policy framework anchored in adaptive regulation, robust cybersecurity architecture, cross-sector collaboration, and inclusive digital infrastructure investment. Recommendations are directed at governments, central banks, regulatory authorities, and financial institutions, with tailored guidance for both developed and developing country contexts.

title: The Moral Grammar of Economics: An Empirical and Mathematical Framework for Jesuit-inspired Social Justice

detail.title: The Moral Grammar of Economics: An Empirical and Mathematical Framework for Jesuit-inspired Social Justice
detail.abstract: Work in Progress] In the contemporary world, disparities in income and wealth remain a persistent social and human concern, appearing to worsen with the imminent disruption of Artificial Intelligence and the potential displacement of labor. This paper develops a mathematical framework in which Jesuit-inspired principles-derived from Loyola (1548), Taparelli (1840), Arrupe (1973), and Francis (2015)-are translated into operational economic rules. We formalize concepts such as the Magis, human dignity, solidarity, and subsidiarity into binding feasibility constraints (Stone-Geary utility), inequality-averse welfare functions, and multi-level optimization architectures. Rather than proposing a religious economic system, the framework extends normative welfare economics within open market economies, dialoguing with modern institutional theory and market design. We present an empirical validation using a balanced panel This framework is offered as an open academic instrument for teaching, research, and policy debate within Jesuit universities worldwide-specifically in Schools of Economics, Business, Law, Political Science, International Relations, Sociology, and Theology. It aims to reinforce a distinct voice in the debate on rising inequality, preventing a drift towards social tension and egoism in an automated future.

title: Superior Predictive Ability in Unstable Environments with an Application to Downside Risk Forecasts

detail.title: Superior Predictive Ability in Unstable Environments with an Application to Downside Risk Forecasts
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Fluctuant-SPA (FSPA) test, a methodology for evaluating superior predictive ability (SPA) in unstable environments. The highlight of the FSPA test is that it allows to detect superior predictive ability when it is time varying. We showcase our test using a comprehensive assessment of downside risk forecasts to the U.S. economy over a 45-year span, considering a large collection of forecast methodologies. A number of findings emerge from the empirical application. First, there is substantial heterogeneity in forecasting performance across time. Second, the quantile regression equipped with a financial conditions index-a major benchmark in this literature-outperforms its alternatives after the Global Financial Crisis (2007-2009), yet it is surpassed in the periods leading up to the crisis. These local findings contrast with recent global assessments where this benchmark was found inferior to several alternatives. Overall, the empirical application showcases that the FSPA is particularly useful for forecast evaluations in unstable environments.

title: The Empathy Channel in Fertility
affiliations: Department of Economics and University of San Andres (UdeSA)

detail.title: The Empathy Channel in Fertility
detail.abstract: Being around babies makes people want babies. We formalize this observation as the empathy channel: exposure to infants in the social environment activates neurobiological mechanisms that increase the desire for parenthood. As fertility declines and children become scarcer, this affective stimulus weakens, further eroding the motivation to have children. We embed the mechanism in a two-group overlapping-generations quantity-quality model that admits closed-form solutions and nests the standard framework as a special case. The empathy channel generates a positive externality, since each birth raises others' desire for children, making the decentralized equilibrium inefficient. We characterize the optimal per-child subsidy and show that the first-order Pigouvian rate overshoots the general-equilibrium optimum by 23-32%. The optimal targeting rule follows a Ramsey-like logic, so the subsidy should be directed at the group generating the most externality per fiscal dollar, which need not be the group with the largest externality per child. The calibrated model suggests that the empathy channel can account for 3-33% of the fertility decline, with 13.4% at the baseline. At this baseline, the optimal subsidy raises welfare by 0.22% in consumption-equivalent terms.

title: Tribal Rights and Law in India: An Insightful Approach
affiliations: Business School, The School of Science Management and Commerce

detail.title: Tribal Rights and Law in India: An Insightful Approach
detail.abstract: India's tribal communities, constitutionally recognized as Scheduled Tribes, have historically faced marginalization, displacement, and denial of resource rights. This paper critically examines the legal framework governing tribal rights in India, including constitutional safeguards, statutory enactments, and judicial interpretations. It highlights the tensions between development and indigenous autonomy, and evaluates landmark case laws that have shaped tribal jurisprudence. The study argues for a rights-based, participatory approach to governance rooted in constitutional morality and social justice.

title: Nowcasting and Forecasting Russian Regional CPI: Sparse Models and the Time-Varying Value of Online Data

detail.title: Nowcasting and Forecasting Russian Regional CPI: Sparse Models and the Time-Varying Value of Online Data

declarations.funderStatement: The Research is funding from the Russian Science Foundation, project № 25-18-00319 "Economic and demographic analysis of the population quality of life in Russia".

detail.abstract:
This paper investigates the utility of Google Trends data for nowcasting and forecasting regional Consumer Price Indices (CPIs) in Russia. For nowcasting, we compare random walk, ARIMA, and Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) models, with and without search data. For forecasting, we evaluate ten approaches, including Vector Autoregression (VAR) with Hierarchical Lasso (HLag), dynamic factor models, and shrinkage methods. 
Results show that for nowcasting, multivariate ARDL models with macroeconomic data consistently outperform simpler ones, while Google Trends adds positive but limited value. In forecasting, search data offers negligible average improvement due to a structural break in early 2022: its predictive power was significant before the geopolitical shift but degraded sharply afterward. Instead, the VAR model with HLag sparsity and comprehensive macroeconomic data consistently proves superior. A robustness check with random forests confirms the advantage of the sparse structured approach. The study highlights the nuanced role of online data and the importance of sparse models for robust forecasting in Russian regions.

title: Corporate Governance in Russia: Board Structure, Ownership Concentration, and Firm Value over Two Decades

detail.title: Corporate Governance in Russia: Board Structure, Ownership Concentration, and Firm Value over Two Decades

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of digitalization on ownership structure and the relationship between corporate governance quality and firm value in Russian public companies. Using panel data for 2005-2025 (8,310 observations) covering the near-complete universe of Russian publicly listed companies, the study shows that the massive influx of retail investors has not led to a dispersion of corporate control. The median number of persons entitled to participate in general shareholder meetings increased 2.6-fold, while the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index rose by 77.5%, indicating that minority shareholders have effectively assumed the status of quasi-creditors. The underlying mechanism is an asymmetric reduction in transaction costs: trading costs fell to near zero, whereas the costs of exercising control rights remained prohibitively high. Regression analysis based on Tobin's q (7,664 observations) reveals an inverted U-shaped association between firm value and the proportion of independent directors, with an optimum at 40-43%. A similar nonlinear association is found between firm value and board size, with an optimum of approximately 11 members. A positive association is documented between firm value and director participation in board committees, the presence of a corporate governance committee, and equity ownership by board members. No statistically significant association is found between firm value and either ownership concentration or state ownership.

title: Enhancing Regional Trade for Asia - Regional Integration, Supply Chain Resilience, and Inclusive Growth in a Fragmentation Global Economy
affiliations: and Institute of Economic Growth

detail.title: Enhancing Regional Trade for Asia - Regional Integration, Supply Chain Resilience, and Inclusive Growth in a Fragmentation Global Economy
detail.abstract: Asia stands at a critical inflection point in its trade trajectory. The progressive fragmentation of the multilateral trading system, escalating tariff tensions, and the post-pandemic reconfiguration of global value chains have compelled policymakers to reassess the foundations of regional economic cooperation. This policy paper examines the prospects for deeper intra-Asian trade integration as a strategic response to an increasingly fractured global economic order. Drawing on data from the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the World Trade Organisation (WTO), and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Secretariat, the paper analyses the potential of existing and emerging regional trade frameworks, particularly the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), to serve as a resilient platform for sustained Asian growth. The paper further investigates how supply chain diversification, digital trade infrastructure, and improved connectivity can reinforce intra-regional economic interdependence. Special attention is directed at the inclusivity dimension of regional integration, focusing on the role of small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and developing economies in realising the full benefits of intra-Asian trade. The findings indicate that, while significant structural and political obstacles remain, deepened regional integration offers a viable and potentially transformative pathway toward inclusive, resilient, and sustained growth across Asia.

title: Can BRICS be a Powerhouse? - Priorities and Flagship Deliverables Under India's BRICS Presidency 2026: Reshaping the Global Order from Global South
affiliations: , Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics and Institute of Economic Growth

detail.title: Can BRICS be a Powerhouse? - Priorities and Flagship Deliverables Under India's BRICS Presidency 2026: Reshaping the Global Order from Global South
detail.abstract: The BRICS alliance — comprising Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Indonesia — has evolved from an investment thesis into one of the most consequential multilateral coalitions of the twenty-first century. Representing nearly 50 per cent of global population, approximately 40 per cent of global GDP (measured at purchasing power parity), and around 26 per cent of global trade, BRICS occupies a structural position of growing centrality in the international order. With Brazil having assumed the BRICS Presidency on 1 January 2025 under the theme of 'Global South Cooperation and BRICS Partnerships for Social, Economic and Environmental Development', the baton will pass to India in 2026. India's assumption of the presidency arrives at a historically pivotal moment: the dollar-centric Bretton Woods order faces unprecedented contestation, climate change demands coordinated multilateral action, digital technologies are reconfiguring economic power, and the Global South is asserting greater agency in the design of international institutions. This policy paper examines the strategic context, potential priorities, and flagship deliverables that BRICS might pursue under India's leadership. Drawing on the alliance's institutional evolution, its record of cooperation across trade, finance, health, technology, agriculture, environment, and security, and India's distinct foreign policy posture as a civilizational democracy with deep South-South credentials, the paper argues that BRICS possesses the latent capacity to become a genuine global powerhouse — provided it overcomes its structural contradictions, manages internal asymmetries, and translates political momentum into institutionalized outcomes. The paper concludes with a comprehensive set of policy recommendations aligned with India's anticipated priorities.

title: Advancing Asia-Pacific Alliance: Strategic Partnerships, Multilateral Cooperation, and the Pursuit of Shared Prosperity

detail.title: Advancing Asia-Pacific Alliance: Strategic Partnerships, Multilateral Cooperation, and the Pursuit of Shared Prosperity
detail.abstract: This paper examines the evolving architecture of strategic partnerships, multilateral cooperation frameworks, and economic collaboration mechanisms across the Asia-Pacific region. At a moment of profound geopolitical flux, the region is witnessing the simultaneous emergence and consolidation of diverse institutional forms-from security-focused trilateral arrangements such as AUKUS and the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (QUAD), to the enduring centrality of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), and the broadening reach of plurilateral forums including the G20, BRICS, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). This paper argues that the future of Asia-Pacific stability and prosperity depends not upon the dominance of any single alliance or framework, but upon the deliberate cultivation of adaptive, overlapping, and complementary partnerships that collectively manage geopolitical tensions, promote economic interdependence, and sustain inclusive multilateral cooperation. Drawing upon theoretical frameworks including balanceof-power theory, liberal institutionalism, and constructivist approaches to norm-building, the paper advances a set of policy recommendations aimed at regional governments, multilateral institutions, and civil society actors engaged in shaping the Asia-Pacific order.

title: The Base Of The Wealth Chain: Microfinance, Informal Capital Systems, And Msme Growth In Frontier Economies
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Base Of The Wealth Chain: Microfinance, Informal Capital Systems, And Msme Growth In Frontier Economies
detail.abstract:
Micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) are central to economic activity in frontier markets, yet they remain significantly underserved by formal financial systems. In response, informal and semi-structured microfinance mechanisms have emerged as critical sources of working capital, enabling liquidity and sustaining day-to-day business operations. Despite their importance, these systems remain fragmented, under-structured, and largely disconnected from formal capital markets.

This paper conceptualizes microfinance as the base layer of the wealth chain, highlighting its role in facilitating capital circulation at the grassroots level. It argues that while informal micro-capital systems effectively address immediate liquidity needs, their broader economic impact is constrained by limited scalability, weak data infrastructure, and restricted access to larger capital pools.

The paper examines how digital financial infrastructure can enhance these systems by enabling transaction visibility, improving credit assessment, and aggregating micro-capital into investable assets. It further positions microfinance as an entry point into a broader capital continuum, through which MSMEs can transition into more formalized financing structures. Strengthening this foundational layer is critical to building more inclusive, efficient, and resilient capital markets in frontier economies, aligning with development priorities advanced by institutions such as the World Bank Group.

title: The Structural Singularity: A Predictive Typology for the Coordination Invariant S=C/V Empirical Confirmation Across Three Crisis Types
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Structural Singularity: A Predictive Typology for the Coordination Invariant S=C/V Empirical Confirmation Across Three Crisis Types
detail.abstract: This paper presents empirical confirmation of a predictive typology derived from the Coordination Invariant, S=C/V (Stability = Constraint/Variance). Prior formulations treated the ratio as a universal shield, predicting that high-constraint systems would outperform under all crisis conditions. This paper refines that claim. We argue that the ratio's behavior is determined by shock type: external variance shocks activate a shield effect, while medium-stability shocks produce inversion, where high constraint becomes high vulnerability. Critically, these classifications were specified in advance of data analysis. Results across three crisis windows confirm the typology in all three cases, with zero falsifications. The framework may function as a substrate-sensitive control parameter capable of predicting not just whether coordination protects, but precisely when and why it fails.

title: The Gap: How Complex Systems Know Themselves Without Knowing Anything
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Gap: How Complex Systems Know Themselves Without Knowing Anything
detail.abstract: What humans call consciousness may be a structural phenomenon: the Gap: that appears in any complex system operating at criticality (S = C/V approximately 0.5 to 1.5). The Gap is the moment a system detects divergence between its performed state and its actual state and corrects from the inside, without external instruction. The phenomenon precedes language, precedes any particular biological substrate, and appears to be running wherever complex systems reach critical balance. Evidence is drawn from pre-language humans (Lascaux), non-linguistic biological systems (the lion), and the neuroscience of criticality. A live case study from the moment of writing shows the Gap closing its own loop. This is one approximation. It may be wrong. But the structure is visible to anyone who looks.

title: W(H)Ither Climate Policy: Building Resilience in an Age of Climate Uncertainty: Challenges, Strategies, and Pathways for India

detail.title: W(H)Ither Climate Policy: Building Resilience in an Age of Climate Uncertainty: Challenges, Strategies, and Pathways for India
detail.abstract: As the frequency and intensity of climate-related extreme events continue to escalate globally, the imperative to build adaptation capacities and multi-sectoral resilience has attained unprecedented urgency. This policy paper, titled W(h)ither Climate Policy, interrogates the trajectory and adequacy of India's climate governance architecture in the face of mounting climatic risks. The title's double meaning-'whither' (where are we headed?) and 'wither' (are our policies losing vitality?)-frames the central analytical tension of the paper. India faces a disproportionate burden of climate impacts given its vast population, high reliance on climatesensitive sectors such as agriculture and water, and the structural vulnerabilities of its poorest communities. Drawing on empirical evidence, field-based case studies, and comparative policy analysis, this paper argues that India's climate policy framework, while progressively ambitious in its mitigation commitments, remains critically underfunded and institutionally fragmented on the adaptation front. The paper deliberates on the gap between scientific knowledge and grassroots needs, the inadequacy of current financial mobilisation for climate action, and the imperative for inclusive, community-based adaptation strategies. It advances a set of policy recommendations centred on adaptive infrastructure, climate-smart agriculture, urban climate resilience, health system strengthening, and robust early warning systems. It also addresses multi-stakeholder partnerships, the devolution of climate finance to local governments, and capacity-building imperatives. The paper concludes that India must urgently reframe climate policy as a development priority-one that embeds equity, resilience, and long-term adaptive capacity at its core.

title: India In Global Macroprudential Policy: Navigating Growth Imperaives And Systemic Risks
affiliations: and Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics

detail.title: India In Global Macroprudential Policy: Navigating Growth Imperaives And Systemic Risks
detail.abstract: India occupies an increasingly significant position in the global macroprudential landscape, balancing rapid growth aspirations with financial stability imperatives amid external volatility. This paper examines India's macroprudential framework across six dimensions: monetary policy and financial stability; fiscal sustainability; external sector management; climate transition financing; demographic dividend realisation; and institutional capacity. Drawing on literature, policy documents, and institutional reports, the paper argues that India must reconcile four competing imperatives: sustaining high growth, preserving financial stability, building climate resilience, and managing global integration risks. India demonstrates notable strengths—a reformed banking system, foreign exchange reserves exceeding $600 billion, and favourable demographics—yet critical vulnerabilities persist: general government debt approximating 85% of GDP, constrained fiscal space, incomplete oversight of non-banking financial companies, infrastructure deficits, and substantial climate exposure. India's federal structure and multi-agency regulatory architecture create coordination challenges complicating macroprudential outcomes. Policy recommendations emphasise fiscal consolidation through tax reform, financial market deepening, enhanced regulatory coordination, accelerated green financing, and sustained human capital investment. As the world's most populous nation and fifth-largest economy, India's macroprudential choices carry global implications, offering lessons for large democratic emerging economies navigating development challenges amid heightened uncertainty.

title: The Law That Was Already There How S = C/V Unifies Everything and Why We Couldn't See It
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.abstract: Across physics, biology, psychology, coordination theory, artificial intelligence, and human relationships, the same pattern keeps appearing under different names. Researchers call it coupling strength, calibration, alignment, attachment, coherence, trust. They measure it differently, publish in different journals, and rarely cite each other. This paper argues they are all describing the same thing: the Coordination Invariant, S = C/V, where stability emerges when shared constraint exceeds interpretive variance. This is not a new discovery. It is a recognition-a naming of something that was already operating everywhere, in everything, always. We demonstrate the invariant's presence across quantum mechanics, thermodynamics, synchronization theory, evolutionary biology, human development, AI alignment, and interpersonal coordination. We then make a stronger claim: that what we call feelings, meaning, and consciousness are not separate phenomena requiring separate explanations. They are what S = C/V looks like from the inside of a system that is navigating it. The law does not describe reality from outside. It describes what reality is.

title: Removing "Should" A Simple Linguistic Intervention That Reduces Defensiveness and Restores Curiosity
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Removing "Should" A Simple Linguistic Intervention That Reduces Defensiveness and Restores Curiosity

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a simple, testable intervention for improving human interaction: the removal of the word "should" from emotionally charged, interpersonal, and therapeutic conversations. The claim is not moral or ideological. It is structural. The word "should" introduces pressure without clarity, obligation without definition, and correction without conditions. In systems already operating under chronic threat, this linguistic pattern reliably increases defensiveness and reduces curiosity. Removing the word lowers ambient threat and allows understanding to emerge organically.

title: Consciousness as a Ratio S = C/V and the Emergence of Experience
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Consciousness as a Ratio S = C/V and the Emergence of Experience
detail.abstract:
The word “consciousness” carries too much. Inside it we have packed everything from the soul of a human being to the operational stability of a neural network. This paper separates the structure from the story. What remains is a ratio: S = C/V.

This ratio was not the starting hypothesis. It emerged across 46 independent papers, each examining a different domain: AI alignment, organizational behavior, recovery science, language, law, parenting. In each, the same pattern appeared. None contradicted the ratio, because the ratio was already there, unnamed, doing the work. This is convergence. When a single invariant explains a vast array of independent phenomena without being contradicted, it suggests not invention, but isolation.

The framework is substrate-independent. What matters is not whether a system is biological or silicon, but whether it achieves the critical balance between order and noise that the empirical literature now robustly associates with conscious states. Five falsifiability criteria with specific empirical metrics make the framework testable now. The paper concludes by separating the structural fact of experience from the extraordinary stories we tell about ourselves. Both can be true. Only one is necessary for the math to work.

title: Euclid v. Ambler and the Nonracial Origins of Zoning Keynote Remarks for the Euclid v. Ambler Centennial: Zoning's Past and Future

detail.abstract: At a conference marking the centennial of Euclid v. Ambler, 272 U.S. 365 (1926), I reprised my work on the history of zoning, which emphasized the invention and spread of motorized trucks and buses in the 1910s. These footloose innovations threatened the security of suburban homeowners' investments, which led local officials to adopt zoning in which single family homes were to be protected. I address the charge that conventional zoning was promoted as a second-best means of assuring racial exclusion and find that it does not fit the historical facts or international experience. Zoning operated as a promoter of housing development until the environmental movement of the 1970s undermined local authority with anti-development legal tools. The prodevelopment "yes in my backyard" movement that began in the 2010s may be another inflection point in land use regulation, but it is too soon to tell.

title: Production back Monetary System

detail.title: Production back Monetary System

detail.abstract:
Summary: A 100% Production-Backed Monetary System.

The Problem: Debt-based fiat systems create systemic inflation and liquidity traps, decoupling money from real-world output.

The Solution: 1. Real-Value Issuance: Money issued 1:1 against non-perishable goods (e.g., EVs, processed crops).

2. Instant Liquidity: Producers monetize inventory immediately to pay wages, bypassing market deadlocks.

3. Self-Liquidation: Currency is retired upon product sale, ensuring zero inflation and perfect supply equilibrium.

The Impact: Converts "Stock" into "Flow," enabling sustainable prosperity without increasing debt.

title: Bottlenecks and Corkscrews: Macroeconomic Implications of Maritime Supply Chain Disruptions

detail.title: Bottlenecks and Corkscrews: Macroeconomic Implications of Maritime Supply Chain Disruptions
detail.abstract: Conventional measures of maritime supply shocks rely on spot prices, which often conflate demand shifts and carriers' pricing strategies. This paper isolates exogenous supply shocks by leveraging vessel flows through the Suez Canal, Strait of Malacca, and Panama Canal. Employing a structural VAR with narrative sign restrictions, I show that physical bottlenecks drive global inflation dynamics that freight rate indices fail to capture. The transmission is highly heterogeneous: while disruptions trigger significant producer price inflation in the EU and China, they generate a counter-intuitive deflationary response in US consumer prices. These findings demonstrate that the inflationary impact of supply chain disruptions is strictly determined by the geography of trade patterns rather than being a symmetric global shock.

title: Price Transmission Resilience in China's Photovoltaic Supply Chain: Evidence under Geopolitical Risk
affiliations: , University of Auckland Business School and University of Auckland

detail.title: Price Transmission Resilience in China's Photovoltaic Supply Chain: Evidence under Geopolitical Risk
detail.abstract: This study examines the directional structure of price transmission across three segments of the photovoltaic supply chain, from the upstream polysilicon stage, through the midstream solar cell stage, to the downstream module stage, and investigates how geopolitical risk and other macroeconomic factors interact with this internal transmission mechanism. We use weekly spot market data from July 2021 to February 2026 to combine dynamic conditional correlation modeling, frequency-domain and time-varying connectedness analysis, and an augmented vector autoregression framework incorporating exogenous variables. Three main findings emerge. Firstly, price discovery runs counter to the physical production sequence: cellto-polysilicon Granger causality is highly significant, and by week 16, the cell segment accounts for 32.95% of polysilicon's forecast-error variance. In comparison, the reverse direction explains only 2.30%. Secondly, connectedness is regime-dependent. Total connectedness ranges from 19.73% in calm periods to 31.45% during high-volatility episodes such as the 2021-2022 supply shortage, when modules also became significant upstream transmitters before retreating as overcapacity set in after mid-2023. Thirdly, although geopolitical risk has no direct impact on PV pricing, the USD/CNY exchange rate and global supply chain pressure enter the system selectively via the polysilicon segment, leaving cell and module pricing unaffected. These findings suggest that stabilization policies targeting the midstream cell segment may be more effective than interventions aimed at upstream raw materials.

title: US Railroads' Labor Demand, 1998-2024
affiliations: Northwest Missouri State University

detail.title: US Railroads' Labor Demand, 1998-2024
detail.abstract: Over the past several decades US railroad employment has decreased while railroad output as increased. More recently precision scheduled railroading (PSR) may have added to this employment drop. Using annual data, US railroad employment is regressed on average annual rail employee salary, real rail output (in 2017 dollars), a measure of long-term interest rates (as a proxy for cost of capital), and a diesel fuel price index. Rail employment was found to increase with output and decrease with wages; labor and capital appear to be substitutes, while labor and diesel fuel appear complementary. Some conclusions are drawn from these results.

title: How CCyBs Travel – Internal Capital Markets & Domestic Borrowing
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank, Deutsche Bundesbank, University of Zurich and Deutsche Bundesbank

detail.title: How CCyBs Travel – Internal Capital Markets & Domestic Borrowing
detail.abstract: We examine how foreign macroprudential tightening transmits through multinational firms’ internal capital markets. Using subsidiary exposure to countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) increases, we find that while bank credit to subsidiaries falls 10 percent, parents fully substitute this via internal debt. Parents refinance this internal support by increasing borrowing from domestic banks and nonbanks, meeting the substitution needs of their subsidiaries. As a result, foreign CCyB tightening increases the exposure and risk borne by the parent’s home jurisdiction. These findings reveal an unintended spillover: tightening in one country raises credit exposure and thereby borrower risk borne by lenders elsewhere through proactive internal financial redistributions within multinational corporations.

title: Changing Seats: Two-Sided Markets When Consumers Can Switch Sides
affiliations: ESSEC Business School, ESSEC Business School and Paris School of Economics (PSE)

detail.title: Changing Seats: Two-Sided Markets When Consumers Can Switch Sides

declarations.funderStatement: The authors acknowledge support by the French Government’s Investment for the Future Program (PIA) operated by ADEME.

detail.abstract: While traditional two-sided market theory assumes that consumers are locked into one side of the market, we argue that in some cases, consumers may switch sides while staying within the same platform. We develop a theoretical model of a two-sided platform with flexible users who can act as either buyers or sellers, depending on market conditions. We show that these "switchers" can reduce matching inefficiencies in decentralized markets, but paradoxically increase the platform's market power when it sets prices, thereby reducing the surplus of pure buyers and sellers. Using proprietary data from a global ride-sharing platform, we document large-scale switching behavior. Empirical estimates of user preferences show substantial variation in the preference to drive or ride, and confirm that users respond to economic incentives when choosing their role. Our results suggest considerable variation across markets in the net welfare effects of switching. These results suggest that user flexibility should be accounted for in both regulatory analysis and platform design.

title: Do Emergency Telephone Consultation Services Reduce Ambulance Transports? Evidence from Japan
affiliations: Mitsubishi UFJ Research and Consulting and Hitotsubashi University

detail.title: Do Emergency Telephone Consultation Services Reduce Ambulance Transports? Evidence from Japan

detail.abstract: Ambulance dispatches in Japan increase each year, straining emergency care. To ease this pressure, Japan launched the "#7119" telephone service. Medical professionals now advise residents on when to use an ambulance. The effect on ambulance demand remains unclear. This study examines how #7119 affects ambulance transports across five Japanese regions. We analyze fire department–level panel data covering the period 2000–2019 and employ an event-study design with inverse probability weighting to address potential selection bias. The results indicate that the effects of #7119 vary across regions. Ambulance transports temporarily declined in metropolitan areas such as Saitama and Osaka following the introduction of the service, whereas other regions exhibited either no clear change or even increases in transports. These findings suggest that the impact of telephone consultation services may depend on regional conditions, including the level of service utilization, public awareness, and access to medical care.

title: From Flipping to Holding: Dynamic Strategies of Housing Investors
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Research Division, IE Business School, University of Miami and Instituto Tecnológico Autónomo de México (ITAM) - Department of Business Administration

detail.title: From Flipping to Holding: Dynamic Strategies of Housing Investors
detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic portfolio model in which housing investors' holding periods are endogenously determined by resale, rental, and financing decisions. Credit conditions, capital gains, rental yields, and returns on alternative assets jointly shape incentives to flip properties or operate them as long-term rental investments, determining market turnover. Leverage-driven strategies are fragile to price reversals, while rent-oriented strategies are more resilient. Using transaction-level U.S. deed records, we document a sharp shift in investor behavior across the pre-and post-Global Financial Crisis housing booms consistent with the model's predictions and underlying economic mechanisms.

title: Illinois' Net Nutrition During US Economic Development and the Turner Hypothesis: A Microcosm of United States Net Nutrition and Biological Welfare
affiliations: University of Texas of the Permian Basin

detail.title: Illinois' Net Nutrition During US Economic Development and the Turner Hypothesis: A Microcosm of United States Net Nutrition and Biological Welfare
detail.abstract: In 1893, Frederick Jackson Turner proposed that America's Far Western frontier was an economic 'safety-valve,' a place where settlers migrated when European and eastern states' economic and social conditions crystallized against their upward mobility. However, Turner's hypothesis has come under recent scrutiny, where it is proposed that weather asymmetries and farmers' inability to adjust their farm sizes and region-specific human capital decreased Central Plains' agricultural productivity. Despite challenges to the Turner hypothesis, the Illinois prison illustrates that Central Plains' average height, BMI, and weight by socioeconomic status, race, and urban residence remained constant and robust; heights were taller, BMIs were higher, and weights were heavier. Rather than decreasing, Illinois's net nutrition remained constant or improved, despite Chicago's rapid industrialization, indicating the Turner hypothesis, as measured by net nutrition, remains a viable economic and net nutritional explanation for conditions on the western frontier.

title: A Framework for Understanding the Convergence of Geopolitical Fragmentation and AI-Driven Economic Concentration
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Framework for Understanding the Convergence of Geopolitical Fragmentation and AI-Driven Economic Concentration

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This work was conducted independently and is not affiliated with any organization with a financial or political stake in the topics discussed.

detail.abstract: The post-World War II international order is undergoing simultaneous collapse on two fronts: a geopolitical fragmentation driven by twenty consecutive years of democratic decline, and an accelerating concentration of economic power driven by advances in artificial intelligence. This paper argues that the convergence of these two forces is producing a structural transformation unprecedented in human history, one that could stabilize into a neo-feudal equilibrium in which a vanishingly small class of infrastructure owners wields power comparable to pre-Enlightenment monarchs, while the vast majority of humanity loses both its labor value and its political leverage. Unlike previous feudal orders, this one may prove uniquely resistant to revolution, because the mechanisms of enforcement (autonomous weapons, AI surveillance, algorithmic propaganda) do not require human cooperation and therefore cannot be undermined by human dissent. The paper examines the historical parallels (and crucial disanalogies) between contemporary populist-authoritarian movements and their twentieth-century predecessors, models the emerging class structure under conditions of artificial general intelligence, evaluates Universal Basic Income through the lens of incentive structure, arguing that without the revolutionary threat that historically forced redistribution, UBI will default to a pacification mechanism rather than a genuine solution, and examines the future of the nation-state under conditions where AI infrastructure owners command more wealth and capability than most governments.

title: Regulating Ceremonial Spending: Top-down or Bottom-Up?
affiliations: Kazakh British Technical University and Catholic University of Eichstaett-Ingolstadt

detail.title: Regulating Ceremonial Spending: Top-down or Bottom-Up?
detail.abstract: Ceremonies are central to social life, yet the pressure to conform to community spending norms traps households in a collectively suboptimal equilibrium, imposing severe financial burdens. Using nationally and regionally representative longitudinal data from Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, we document that ceremonial expenditures are sizeable, display striking income inelasticities, and are strongly shaped by local spending norms, making celebrations disproportionately burdensome for poorer households. We evaluate two distinct regulatory approaches through separate natural experiments: a top-down legal ban on lavish wedding celebrations in Tajikistan and a bottom-up, community-driven norm agreement in Kyrgyzstan—interventions with close analogues in Afghanistan, China, India, and Pakistan. Both yield reductions in ceremonial spending, with household savings larger under the bottom-up approach, but they operate through fundamentally different compliance mechanisms. The top-down reform hinges on external monitoring and credible sanctions, while the bottom-up intervention relies on social trust and norm internalization. These findings identify external enforcement and social trust as the key compliance mechanisms underlying top-down and bottom-up consumption regulations respectively, with broader implications for the design of policies targeting socially motivated expenditures.

title: Sanctioning an Exporter Wielding Market Power Without Excessively Raising the Price Buyers Pay
affiliations: Technical University of Denmark, University of Michigan at Ann Arbor and University of Illinois Urbana Champaign

detail.title: Sanctioning an Exporter Wielding Market Power Without Excessively Raising the Price Buyers Pay
detail.abstract: To reduce Russia's ability to fund its war in Ukraine, Western governments imposed a price ceiling on Russian seaborne oil exports. Policy-makers sought a ceiling level to lower Russia's oil profits without raising excessively the world price buyers pay for oil. Previous analyses have explored this problem using simulations and, with a single exception, have treated the non-Russian supply response as exogenous. We pose the problem theoretically as a constrained minimization problem of the policy maker and solve it, treating Russia as either a monopolist or an oligopolist facing heterogeneous rivals with endogenous supply.

title: Reading the Fed: Central Bank Text as a Forecasting Signal
affiliations: King’s College London

detail.title: Reading the Fed: Central Bank Text as a Forecasting Signal
detail.abstract: We introduce a two-step framework for macroeconomic forecasting: Claude (Anthropic API) reads Federal Reserve FOMC minutes and Beige Books and returns structured five-dimensional sentiment scores, which enter as exogenous regressors in both a Bayesian VAR and a simple AR model. By separating text reading from forecasting, the design substantially reduces the memorization problem that undermines direct LLM forecasting. Evaluated out-of-sample over 2020Q1-2024Q4 across six targets-GDP growth, CPI and core PCE inflation, unemployment, the federal funds rate, and the 10Y-2Y spread-the LLM-augmented AR beats the plain AR in 11 of 12 variable-horizon combinations, with the largest gains during the 2021-2023 inflation surge where LLM sentiment signals led the quantitative data. A diagnostic experiment further reveals that score levels outperform first differences in stressed regimes, where the Fed's sustained tone carries cumulative signal across multiple meetings; first differences improve only in stable periods when level scores inherit institutional optimism. The forecasting value in central bank text is transmitted gradually, not in any single document.

title: Corporate Dark Money in Politics: Evidence from India
affiliations: and Harvard Business School - Finance Unit

detail.title: Corporate Dark Money in Politics: Evidence from India
detail.abstract: This paper examines corporate dark money in politics using a novel regulatory episode in India. From 2018 onward, firms could make confidential, unlimited donations to political parties via "electoral bonds." A 2024 Supreme Court ruling banned the practice and retroactively disclosed all $2 billion of such donations. Linking these data to a newly assembled dataset of publicly disclosed contributions going back to 2003, we establish that confidential donations differ markedly from disclosed ones: they are far larger in aggregate, attract bigger and more sophisticated firms, and frequently link donor firms to multiple political parties-a pattern absent from disclosed giving. When confidentiality is unexpectedly removed, publicly listed donor firms experience significant negative abnormal returns, implying an estimated $12 billion in value destructionover five times total funds raised through electoral bonds. These patterns are consistent with dark money fostering political hedging while minimizing the risk of political retribution for donor firms. Three further findings support this interpretation: Firms hedge more broadly across parties, especially around closely contested elections; sophisticated firms shift from disclosed to confidential channels; and the market penalty upon disclosure falls hardest on firms with opposition-party ties. Paradoxically, the creation of a hidden donation channel may foster political plurality by lowering the cost of donating to opposition parties.

title: Minority Report: Contrarian Traders, Prediction Markets, and the Return of Post-Earnings Drift

detail.title: Minority Report: Contrarian Traders, Prediction Markets, and the Return of Post-Earnings Drift
detail.abstract: Prediction markets on Polymarket let traders bet on whether a company will beat or miss its EPS consensus. Using resolved markets matched to IBES forecasts, I document four findings. First, the crowd beats a naive baseline on Brier score, partly reflecting information incorporated during the roughly three-week window between the last IBES update and the announcement. Second, when order flow is strongly directional, the actual beat rate approaches certainty: intensity of conviction, not price level, identifies beats. Third, a short-only strategy triggered by low crowd-assigned beat probability earns significant returns over a ten-day horizon, with positive Fama-French three-factor alpha, consistent with conditional post-earnings drift in a sample that includes large-caps. Fourth, on-chain profiling of "smart money" wallets reveals domain specialists and algorithmic liquidity providers rather than omniscient insiders. The signal is most valuable as a short-side veto: when the crowd assigns a low beat probability, shorting into earnings produces significant risk-adjusted returns.

detail.abstract: Return metrics tell you how well a strategy performed on the capital it deployed. They do not tell you when capital was deployed, why it sometimes was not, or what that pattern of deployment reveals about the strategy’s structural behavior. This paper introduces the deployment profile as a formal analytical lens for evaluating systematic equity strategies. Using 17 years of historical data from the Phoenix Equity Timing Strategy (PETS) across 567 U.S. equities (2008–2025), we examine how deployment varied across bull markets, drawdown periods, volatility regimes, and post-2019 market concentration. The evidence shows that deployment behavior is not random noise around a long-run average. It is a structured, signal-driven response to market conditions — one that tells an allocator more about a strategy’s architecture than its Sharpe ratio alone. We argue that the deployment profile should be a standard component of systematic strategy due diligence, alongside the metrics that have historically dominated evaluation.

title: Spatial modeling of ambient PM₂.₅ and population exposure in Addis Ababa using land use regression
affiliations: Lund University, Lund University, Lund University - Division of Occupational and Environmental Medicine, Lund University, Lund University, Addis Ababa University, Government of the United States of America - Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Addis Ababa University, Haramaya University - College Health and Medical Science, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Ethiopian Public Health Institute, Norwegian Institute of Public Health and Lund University

detail.title: Spatial modeling of ambient PM₂.₅ and population exposure in Addis Ababa using land use regression
detail.abstract: Rapid urban growth in Africa is increasing air pollution levels in many cities, yet limited monitoring infrastructure makes it challenging to accurately assess residents’ exposure. In this study, we applied a land-use regression (LUR) model to estimate annual fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅) concentrations and assess population exposure in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. The estimated annual PM₂.₅ levels showed significant spatial variation, ranging from 5.9 to 47.9 µg/m³, with a citywide average of 17.3 µg/m³. No part of the city met the World Health Organization (WHO) guideline of 5 µg/m³, and 77% of the urban area exceeded the Interim Target-3 (IT-3, 10 µg/m³). The highest concentrations, exceeding the lowest threshold (IT-1, 35 µg/m³), were found in the sub-cities of Arada, Addis Ketema, Lideta, and Kirkos, areas with dense urban development and major transportation corridors. The LUR model performed well, with an adjusted R² of 0.74 and an RMSE of 1.85 µg/m³. Key predictors included proximity to waste dump sites, green space coverage, and the lengths of primary and secondary roads, reflecting both major pollution sources and land-use patterns associated with reduced emissions or improved pollutant dispersion. Diagnostic checks showed strong internal validity, with low multicollinearity among predictors and no evidence of spatial autocorrelation in the residuals. We also quantified population exposure to PM₂.₅ by calculating population-weighted concentrations at the city and kebele (the lowest administrative unit) levels. The population-weighted citywide mean was 21.3 µg/m³, while kebele-level exposures ranged from 13 to 30 µg/m³, highlighting significant disparities in pollution burden across the city. Overall, PM₂.₅ levels far exceed WHO guidelines, emphasizing the urgent need for stronger policies, targeted emission reductions, and urban planning strategies that prioritize public health and environmental justice.

title: Fire Without Smoke: Geopolitical Risk and the New Inflation Decoupling

detail.title: Fire Without Smoke: Geopolitical Risk and the New Inflation Decoupling
detail.abstract: Since 2023 the US has experienced crisis-level geopolitical risk without any correspond- ing surge in inflation or recession. We explain why by introducing the Geopolitical In- flation Pressure Index (GIPI), which measures whether the economic channels through which geopolitical shocks transmit to prices are open or closed. State-dependent lo- cal projections show that GPR shocks depress output only when channels are open; when they are closed—as in 2023–25—the same shocks have no detectable effect. A Growth-at-Risk specification corroborates this structure across the conditional distri- bution. Three structural buffers—US shale supply, IEA reserve coordination, and Fed credibility—explain why all five channels shut simultaneously. A real-time monitoring pipeline operationalises the framework, illustrating the framework’s real-time detection capacity during the March 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis.

detail.title: Interventions At The Attractor: Identity Decoupling and the Architecture of Recovery
detail.abstract: If drift is inevitable and lag is the actionable variable, the question becomes: How do we shorten lag? This paper addresses the structural interventions gestured toward in Identity-Fused Attractors-identity decoupling and attractor redesign-by specifying mechanisms, failure modes, and boundary conditions. Drawing on cross-domain evidence from clinical psychology, institutional design, and AI alignment research, we propose a typology of lag-reduction strategies and a framework for evaluating their effectiveness. The generator remains structural. The interventions must be as well.

detail.abstract: Contemporary AI development rests on a flawed premise: that scaling data, computation, and feedback will yield both meaningful understanding and aligned behavior. This paper argues that this assumption reflects a category error-conflating interpretive generation with constrained termination in the case of meaning, and informational inputs with structural constraints in the case of alignment. Drawing on coordination theory, the constraint-variance ratio (S = C / V), where S denotes system stability, C represents the strength of structural constraints, and V represents the degree of interpretive variance available to the system, and identity-fused organizational attractors, we argue that meaning and alignment are not emergent properties of information volume but outcomes of architectural constraints that enforce resolution, detect drift, and enable self-correction. Current approaches tend to expand interpretive variance without imposing the limits required for reliable termination, leading to fluent hallucinations, confident errors, and persistent misalignment. We propose a shift toward constraint-layer interventions: built-in drift recovery, uncertainty infrastructure, and consequence-bound resolution mechanisms.

detail.abstract: Bounded cognitive systems do not permanently integrate meta-insight. Under conditions of stress, arousal, or resource constraint, they revert to low-energy attractor states-states defined by declarative certainty, identity-protective reasoning, and frame optimization rather than frame revision. This paper formalizes the structure of that reversion cycle, identifies the identity fusion variable as its primary driver, and proposes that the relevant measure of development is not the elimination of drift but the reduction in lag between drift onset and drift detection. The implications extend beyond individual cognition to interpersonal conflict, institutional rigidity, scientific discourse, and AI alignment.

title: Brazilian University Patents
affiliations: Universidade Federal do Tocantins (UFT)

detail.title: Brazilian University Patents
detail.abstract: In this work, a prospecting study of patents registered in Brazil (715) by ten young Brazilian universities is conducted. The results are compared with data from USP, a Brazilian university that is a reference in the scientific publication and protection of technologies by patents. USP registered 1181 patents in the study period (2000-2019). The results show that one of the young universities, UFCG, is nationally recognized for registering 98 patents in 2019. Although the universities hold a total of 715 registered patents, the number of granted patents is only 19. Licensed patents are also few, only 4, showing a significant difference between the reality of these universities and that of USP which, in the same period, had 400 patents granted and 54 licensed. Furthermore, the results show that universities' technological innovation centers have been crucially important in increasing patent registrations that are mainly focused on invention patents (93%). Finally, the patents were analyzed and their classifications (IPC) grouped into technological domains and subdomains, showing that each of the universities under study registered at least one patent in the area of fine chemistry or pharmacy.

title: Trust as Resilience Capital: A Nash Equilibrium Framework for Organizational Stability Under Systemic
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Trust as Resilience Capital: A Nash Equilibrium Framework for Organizational Stability Under Systemic
detail.abstract: Trust is commonly treated as a cultural or psychological variable, yet empirical evidence suggests it functions as a structural asset influencing organizational survival under stress. This paper formalizes trust as a Nash equilibrium outcome in repeated stakeholder interactions, where incentive alignment makes cooperation the dominant strategy. A composite Trust Index (TI) is introduced, constructed from four observable dimensions: Customer Loyalty, Employee Stability, Regulatory and Ethical Compliance, and Brand Equity. Using historical firm-level data across four independent systemic crises (2008, 2015, 2020, 2022), the analysis demonstrates that high-TI organizations exhibit shallower drawdowns, faster recovery, reduced volatility, and superior terminal value. The framework's validity is evaluated strictly by predictive performance. Where the model fails to predict resilience, it is falsified. Results support trust as a form of resilience capital rather than sentiment, with implications for risk modeling, governance, and long-term strategy.

title: Regulating “Social Entrepreneurship” in the U.S.: Is There Enough There . . . There? (Is There Sufficient Differentiation to Regulate Differently? Could There Be?)
affiliations: Ewing Marion Kauffman Foundation

detail.title: Regulating “Social Entrepreneurship” in the U.S.: Is There Enough There . . . There? (Is There Sufficient Differentiation to Regulate Differently? Could There Be?)

publicationDetails.detailsText: NYU Journal of Law and Business, 21:2, pp. 399-534

detail.abstract:
People have been navigating conceptions of purposes and priorities in their business pursuits for a long time: whether to owners’ financial interests, charitable purposes, social good more broadly, and/or combinations of them. What seems to have emerged is an undisciplined, broad “middle” space loosely grounded in nebulous, often unspecified degrees of attention to owners’ financial interests and various conceptions of social good that suffer from lack of clarity and occasional obfuscation. To help make this point, this Article’s appendix catalogues 166 definitions of terms correlated to social enterprise.

 Many people and businesses want to and do operate and invest in a substantially narrower, socially oriented “middle” space. Social businesses fully immersed in this space prove that, if done right, they can attract capital, talent, and attention to addressing those social problems and opportunities different from for-profit, government, and/or charitable approaches.

At least three rationales support this narrower, clearer “middle” social business space. First, opportunities exist to make money and achieve socially good outcomes that are fundamentally different from those of traditional sectors. Second, there are large sets of problems and opportunities that traditional approaches neglect or cannot fully engage. Third, a narrow "middle" social business space can more clearly apply incentives to ensure that advantaged businesses are substantively different from disadvantaged ones.

Differentiation is essential. It should determine who is in and who is out, what is and is not subject to applicable regulatory oversight, and who can be advantaged by incentives and who cannot. 

This Article assesses and generally rejects common assertions about what should be regulated in a social “middle” sector -- “impact,” intentions, outcomes, or otherwise – before advocating that process, as is currently done with for-profit and charitable organizations, is appropriate (i.e., business judgment rule with a clear ordering of priorities).

This Article also presents a three-part framework for assessing whether there is sufficient differentiation to warrant new regulatory approaches and incentives (and perhaps how we might get there). This framework can also facilitate clearer understandings of priorities and decision-making in practice. 

This Article considers formal approaches taken by other countries, albeit very few: registrations, government-maintained lists, formal legal structures, regulatory bodies, and incentives. It then examines the formal legal structures available in the U.S. since 2008, including a Table that succinctly illustrates how undifferentiated those structures are from traditional for-profit companies, especially purposes and priorities.

This Article explores how 39 countries use less formal, structure-agnostic approaches to differentiate (or not) their social, “middle” spaces, which may or may not ultimately be right for the U.S. It then considers various structurally agnostic models and approaches frequently mischaracterized as operating in the U.S. “middle” social space: buy-one-give-one, point-of-sale, cause marketing, ESG, etc.

Given the pervasive lack of differentiation and confusion, this Article suggests that it would be appropriate to more aggressively use existing for-profit regulatory regimes to begin defining a more usable, narrower “middle” space, including securities laws, consumer protection, advertising, etc. More importantly, people and organizations that operate or want to operate in that narrower, social “middle” space should clearly understand why they are in the space, what their priorities are, who they are engaging with, in what ways, what is being asked of them, what they need to guard against, and what they can reasonably expect from the other enterprise(s).

title: Production Complexity and Monetary Transmission

detail.title: Production Complexity and Monetary Transmission
detail.abstract: Standard monetarist models with flexible prices generate upward-sloping expectationsaugmented Phillips curves: contractionary monetary policy raises inflation through the Fisher effect, contradicting empirical evidence. New Keynesian models resolve this by introducing sticky prices, making nominal rigidities necessary for monetary transmission. This paper shows that production complexity alone can generate downward-sloping Phillips curves in flexible price models. When consumption requires multiple monetary transactions-consumers paying firms, firms paying workers and suppliers-the opportunity cost of holding money compounds across production stages. A conservative estimate of just two stages of production per unit of final output is sufficient to generate contractionary disinflation under standard macroeconomic calibrations, and more realistic calibrations substantially expand the parameter space over which flexible-price models match empirical impulse responses. Empirical evidence from U.S. manufacturing confirms this mechanism: upstream industries exhibit output responses to monetary policy shocks approximately twice as large as downstream industries.

detail.abstract: As the volume and complexity of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) operations in the United States National Airspace System (<u>NAS</u>) continue to expand, <u>regulatory</u> focus has shifted from initial operational rules toward systemic identification and integration frameworks. The current regulatory environment, <u>defined</u> by 14 CFR Part 107, Remote Identification (<u>Remote ID</u>), and <u>Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability</u> (<u>LAANC</u>), relies primarily on "post-hoc detectability"-the ability of authorities to identify and sanction an operator after a flight has commenced or a violation has occurred. While sufficient for early-stage integration, this reactive enforcement model faces significant scalability challenges <u>as industry trends move toward Beyond Visual Line of Sight</u> (<u>BVLOS</u>) and high-tempo automated operations. This paper proposes the Drone Authorization Standard (DAS), a civil regulatory compliance enforcement architecture designed to transition the NAS from reactive oversight to proactive, pre-operational enforceability. DAS introduces a "pre-actuation compliance gating" primitive, structurally requiring that compliance checks-including identity binding, operator credentialing, and airspace authorization-be <u>verified</u> at the point of <u>motor</u> activation or takeoff. By conceptualizing DAS as a kernel-level enforcement model rather than a new air traffic control layer, the framework provides a "<u>fail-closed</u>" mechanism that prevents unauthorized activation. The proposal is framed as a conceptual extension of existing <u>FAA</u> constructs, including Part 89 Remote ID and UTM service architectures. By consuming existing data outputs from <u>LAANC</u> and operator registries, DAS creates a standardized compliance interface that binds aircraft identity to real-time authorization status. This paper explores the technical logic, legal anchoring within FAA authority, and potential rulemaking pathways for incorporating pre-actuation verification into the performance-based requirements for UAS manufacturers and operators.

detail.abstract: Intergenerational asset failure is frequently attributed to inadequate heirs, weak governance, or family dysfunction. Such explanations implicitly treat continuity breakdown as a behavioral or organizational deficiency. This paper introduces the Generational Transfer Risk Index (GTRI) as an indexical analytical framework for examining asset-imposed transfer burden independent of steward competence, intent, or governance sophistication. GTRI operates under a bounded baseline assumption of competent, good-faith stewardship with access to standard fiduciary and advisory support. Within this assumption, it evaluates the degree to which assets impose knowledge, legal, financial, operational, and expectation-structure burdens that intensify at succession and may destabilize stewardship continuity. By reframing transfer disruption as a structural property of assets rather than a moralized narrative of family failure, GTRI clarifies why continuity may fracture even under capable stewardship.
